paragraphs.text: To his holy and most blessed lord, his special patron before God, worthy of all reverence and wonder, and a truly apostolic teacher in every part of religion, Bishop Perpetuus: from Paulinus.

Out of eager charity and loving affection you bid me forget my modesty, although you urge modesty and restraint on others, so that judgment may not be weighed down by transgression. You do not see that you are mistaken, judging more kindly than truly: you believe a thing good because you wish it good, and you admit into the fellowship of your devotion even people you have chosen from among the foolish. You sent us so splendid an account of the merits and mighty works of our holy and apostolic teacher and lord that it would most rightly have reached the knowledge of the whole world, had your blessing so ordered. But you have judged that I should follow in these footsteps and could add something more polished, as it were, whereas it is a far greater thing to bring out what one has discovered than to copy out what has already been published. Still, let us agree to submit in obedience and not weigh our own conscience too rashly, for I think one ought not to question what is commanded by a man to whom all one's wishes to obey are subject. Holy and most blessed lord, true patron of perpetual religion and grace, mirror of venerable doctrine, model of perfection: follow him whom you love, imitate him whom you follow, his successor in office, his venerator in humility.

Let us keep to the terms of your command. Claim what is yours, for, as you know, it was by this choice of yours that you made me answerable. When the paper reaches your hands, cherish what you receive, excuse my lack of skill, and entreat his clemency: may he pardon my presumption, help a sinner, and come to the aid of my error. It was unfitting for us to dare to touch such great deeds, but it would have been more arrogant to scorn your commands. May he patiently bear the murmurings that were undertaken out of grace, and not be angry at a boldness made stronger by joy. Our God wishes the things he deigns to work through Martin to be made known, whoever announces them. Cherish with your patronage the man you have taken up, whom you adopted, though unknown, through those treasures of charity.
BOOK ONE.
Christ had spread his venerable light through all the world,
unlocking the mysteries of the gospel kingdom.
But since the working of his mighty deeds had not moved
every nation, and with frail understanding they hesitated to believe
whatever a messenger had published from foreign shores
(for things learned by hearsay move us by words, things present by deeds:
things unseen may persuade, but things seen are proved),
he, then, whose mercy is equal toward the whole world,
sowed many miracles in our lands as well,
granting the glories of Martin to the farthest Gauls.
Fertile Pannonia sent him from afar for our salvation,
born of no humble stock, the son of a tribune.
His father was renowned for the praise of his merits; but the son
was nobler than such famous forebears, for, with Christ as his father,
he spurned sacrilegious rites, nobly unlike his father.
For scarcely in his tenth year, already old in character,
he crossed over to the sacred law with a steadfast heart
and marked his holy brow with the protection of the cross.
There was no fickle mind in his tender breast: his whole
desire was to keep and to know the command of God,
to shun the gatherings of men, to learn the secrets of the blessed
desert, and, scorning the world, to know God,
and to leave earthly cares behind with a lofty heart.
While he was attempting this at barely twelve years old,
the lofty glory of so great a deed was barred to him,
yet God counted it as merit, for he approved the will.
The emperor ordered that, by a levy to prepare for war,
all the sons of veterans' stock should be enlisted.
What will envy not do? His father betrays him and thrusts arms
upon his son. Alas, a father's love forgetful of so great a danger!
Rather, father, if your stony mind admits any feeling,
grow through your son's honours: for it is greater praise for you to be surpassed.
See only what he achieved in all things by his devout vow:
if they are good, imitate them gladly; if too hard, rejoice in them.
Christ's soldier is bound in place of a soldier of the world,
but his mind is not dragged along, nor is his heart bound with his flesh.
The titles of a recruit are empty: he had long been a soldier,
he who, won by his own King through many battles,
had conquered greed and vanquished proud
luxury; ambition already lies laid low by his strength,
and rage and anger flee his steadfast mind,
as does deadly pride, worse than all faults.
Going forth, he scarcely allows a single companion to go with him,
a servant bound not by labour but in name alone.
O happy man, for whom so pleasing a condition prepared such a yoke
that the rival wishes of noble men
might contend with you for your lot,
if only they were allowed to serve! But you too
are forced under a hard law, though freed from the law of your birth:
for the devotion of the saint serves you, his subordinate.
The same dress, the shared plenty of a frugal table;
he was the first to serve, so that no shrewdness could even detect
that the servant had been placed above his master.
And what graciousness he showed among his equals, and how modestly
true love had made him subject even to his superiors!
Then how strict his restraint in taking food,
lest a bloated belly dull his quick sense
and the burden of the body weigh down his wakeful mind,
so that his plenty, divided, might give a share to the needy,
and what would overload one might better refresh both.
For he had so divided everything among the poor who begged of him
that only a covering remained for his wasted limbs,
when suddenly, in the icy cold of bristling winter,
a naked man hurries to meet him, scarcely half-uttering words
broken off by his shivering; but his plight
frees his speech, and his distress cries out the part his tongue could not.
Everyone passes by, and the folly of the rich
scorned his loathsome complaint with wretched laughter.
The saint stood still, uncertain, his heart perplexed
as to what to do: for the wish was there, the means were not.
If he covered the man, he himself would be stripped. Yet even so
his hesitation did not hold back his famous deed by the slightest delay.
All that was left to cover his blessed body
was his cloak, doubled as always, which with its twofold wrap
kept off cold and rain and the fury of the winds.
For the hanging fold makes up for the part cut short,
if what is lacking at the head the body feels has gone to its warmth,
warmed by the added wool.
But the happy judgment of his strict vow
sets this aside and condemns as a loss to his heart
that the timid caution of faith should prefer
to give the part added to his limbs by the doubled covering
to one alone rather than divide it between two.
No delay slows the work; his right hand outstrips his wish
and carried out whatever his mind saw must be done.
His unconquered sword is drawn, guiltless of any wound,
and lavish compassion cuts the cloak through the middle,
choosing, I believe, the worse half for himself. Then he covers
the trembling man's limbs, and, giving away some warmth from his garment,
in his now lighter dress he takes on a share of the cold.
O happy man, by your virtue surpassing all
miracles and going beyond the precepts of the Lord who commands!
For he bids us be content with little
and not to keep two garments: you divide one.
Everyone looks on. Some laugh at the unsightly
covering and do not see the truer beauty in his heart.
But others, pricked in heart, lament to themselves
that a poor man's justice could grant to the needy
what ample means with a rich estate had refused.
Without delay the palm is awarded for so great a triumph.
For hardly had he laid his weary limbs upon his bed,
admitting a light sleep, yet with a wakeful heart
(nor was it sleep, for his attentive mind was alert),
when suddenly before his eyes, kindly, with a rich reward,
there stood Christ, clothed in the person of his poor one,
and he fitted the blessed covering to his own limbs.
O truly precious cloak! What garments, renowned for purple
or for gold drawn into thread in glowing skeins,
ever earned such honour? What silks, smooth to the touch,
or alive with skilfully worked figures?
He, the God of men and earth, of sea and sky,
who has given all things, without whom there is nothing, and to whom belong
both what we have given and we who gave, both gift and giver,
is enriched by this help, if he counts the gains of salvation.
Yet not even this caused vanity to shake his steady mind,
nor did he feel any empty swelling in his heart.
O virtue close to God: to count nothing as praise
while doing what is praiseworthy, not to credit to our own doing
what we do, and to have God praised in every act!
By now he was surely secure in so great a judge,
yet he is not puffed up even by fellowship with Christ:
the vision strengthens his faith; renewed in the holy washing,
his limbs shine and take on a beauty equal to his heart's,
and the mysteries of the font give birth to a new body.
And yet, though he shone with this maturity of character and of body,
he had lived only four lustres less two years;
I truly believe it was because the Holy Spirit had first
enriched his whole heart with the river of his watering gift,
as holy Peter once saw blessed gifts
sent ahead by the Lord upon just such a soldier.
Who, I ask, however good, will be able to finish as well
as blessed Martin began in his tender years?
And yet, doing all this, he thought he had not even begun,
because for barely two years he had delayed a little,
already a monk in merit, but a soldier in name only,
in breaking off the empty titles of the world he had trampled on,
waiting for the holy fellowship of the tribune who had promised it,
so that, with Christ soon to be judge, a small and just delay
might be made good by a twofold salvation through the vows of two.
Meanwhile, the barriers broken and the frontier breached,
a savage enemy had begun to lay waste the Gallic countryside.
The emperor makes ready to go and meet him, and all the companies,
summoned by command, exhortation, entreaty, and largesse,
he gathers for war. For those whom fear holds back
are tempted by rewards, and gifts overcome fear.
But a mind full of God fears nothing, scorns everything,
laughs at terror, and tramples earthly rewards underfoot.
So when those ahead of him had taken their gift,
as the line went on, the saint is called up in the usual way.
He rejects the gifts the emperor offers there before him,
and with these words answers the tyrant's words:
"Give these earthly gifts, these coins, to someone else, emperor:
greater rewards from a greater King await me.
This is the wage of war: let those who wish to fight take it."
At these words the emperor blazes into fierce anger,
charging that, a coward in time of war
and heedless of glory, he had invented excuses for his fear.
But Martin replied: "I have no fear of the danger at hand,
nor do steadfast hearts dread an easy death.
In short, what words declare, deeds too will prove.
I will go first before the ranks, my weapons cast aside,
taking up not the arms of men but the signs of salvation,
trusting not in the cover of a shield but in the name of Christ,
and setting the cross on my brow for aid instead of a helmet,
and with fearless heart I will face every danger."
The emperor agreed, and so that proof might confirm the truth of his words,
the devout man is ordered kept under harsh guard.
And now the newly risen day was scattering its first light
over the earth: a suppliant embassy comes to the emperor,
bowing their necks in submission to his rule.
What, I ask, do we see achieved here by men, what by arms?
What did the iron battle line avail, what terror and the sword?
What column fell to javelins, what squadron to arrows?
One man, and trust in the eternal King alone,
conquered countless peoples without the wound of slaughter.
Here, Martin, was your triumph, with Christ fighting for you,
so that you would not stain your holy face with blood at all
and the deaths of the dying would not afflict your devout mind.
So, eager in merit and made keener by success itself,
his enemies overcome, he hastens to conquer the world.
He seeks out Hilary, a teacher of the faith proven by so many
proofs. Lest vanity inflict any wound
or the opinion of his own heart exalt him,
though already a teacher he plays the disciple, and proves the greater
by wishing to be the lesser: for to scorn praise is praise.
So too, though already worthy of the honour of a bishop's chair,
he refused even to be distinguished with the honour of deacon,
and only reluctantly took a place he had long since surpassed by holy living,
asking for lower duties for himself:
an exorcist in rank, but already a priest in virtue.
Then, lest even earthly duty should find fault with him,
whom divine love guided so especially,
he longs with eager wish to visit his parents
and, better still, to turn their averted minds.
For a headlong and wayward error weighed down his father and mother,
who practised sacrilegious rites and worshipped stone and bronze,
living under an all too powerful death.
So filial love went with him as companion on his journey, and an angel
sent by the Lord had smoothed every region ahead of him,
so that a gentle ascent lay open, the hill brought low,
and cliffs and hollows did not drag him down into headlong falls.
And while he was swiftly crossing the cloud-bearing Alps,
he happened to be caught in an ambush of savage robbers;
with his hands bound behind his back, facing their threatening swords,
he smiled and scorned the danger with an unmoved face.
Indeed, to recall the wonders of so great a deed,
he is said to have saved his guard by counsels of salvation,
he the truer guard of the soul, the other merely of the body.
For the one did not even hold the limbs he guarded in his power,
while the other bound the inmost depths of a hostile mind.
Yet both skilfully showed the way to follow:
the one showed the road along the highway, and learned the road of salvation.
So he completes the journey he had begun and draws near his homeland,
having crossed the Alps and entered the fields of Italy.
Here again the enemy, ever opposed to holy endeavours,
feigning human form in a counterfeit body,
placed himself in his path, daring to ask him
where he was going and what this haste was for.
Martin answered: "My only way and guide is Christ: in him
lies the fulfilment of my purpose [?], for he gave me the will."
But the demon, gnashing his teeth, said he would stand in the way of all his efforts,
offended at so great an undertaking.
The saint replied: "The Lord defends; the enemy does no harm:
with God as helper no hostile power
can be feared. Fearing the Lord, I scorn danger.
It is that fear which makes me unafraid." When he had spoken
these words, the phantom was driven off and vanished from his sight.
And when, with the Lord as guide, he reached his parents' country,
though perdition, hardened by the persuasion of habit, still held his father,
who rejected the words of salvation pressed on him,
yet at least, by Christ's gift, he won back his mother.
O woman blessed in so great an offspring, who bore a son
through whom she was born to God, and by a single birth
became both mother and child! The mother, herself yet to be born,
first bore from her womb the blessed one through whom she is now born of the font.
Many others, too, yielded to his saving example,
rightly marvelling at the marks of so great a character.
At that time the evil error of a deadly doctrine
had spread among peoples who followed it with unwary hearts
the poison that Arius had poured from his mad mouth.
This plague held Illyricum infected above all,
having raged through it entirely with its venom.
Here, strong in steadfast virtue, he dared to stand against it
and broke its waves with his breast set against them,
often rebuking the priests and often the people;
overwhelmed by everyone's plots, having suffered beatings,
driven out, he at last left those earthly dwellings,
yet he kept the faith on his lips and salvation in his heart.
So when he judged he must withdraw, lest, if he lingered,
the madness of a world overturned should overwhelm the saint,
he made again for the Gallic countryside and retraced the steps
he had marked before, never forgetful of the faith.
But since deadly error was raging throughout the world
and these crimes were pressing hard on the farthest Gauls,
and since the faction of a mad world had driven out
Hilary himself, the wall of faith and its strong pillar,
he decided to rest a while in a cell he had built
here, where Italy, rejoicing in the shade of groves and vines,
is adorned by most beautiful Milan.
Driven from here too he departs, leaving lands and city walls
and making for the sea and its waves, since the water was more faithful
as a host, and the storm of the crowd and the mob
was more to be feared than that of the sea. With him on his way went
a priest of the same merit and in like danger.
An island is chosen as their lodging, far from any host.
Herbs suffice for food. Living on their roots,
the saints double their fasts with so barren a diet.
And while, without discrimination, they search for meagre food,
whatever the bowels of unfamiliar earth provided,
they suddenly felt the herb hellebore, with its poison,
spreading deadly venom through all their limbs.
They turn to the Lord with all the power of prayer,
but his kindness came before their prayers. No art was employed;
the only remedy at hand was the hope of salvation.
Let us consider, we who are used to seeking life with our whole fortune,
pouring out our money in fees to doctors
so that the span of our living may grow through our coins,
what potions of choice juices achieved here,
or remedies once culled from ancient books.
Here, surely, without expense or skill, the heart won swift healing
and the word bestowed it: let us marvel and rejoice.
The voice is silent, and the case is pleaded by the cry of the silent.
The physician is felt, not seen: all their limbs,
though their pores are closed, admit the cure to their inmost parts.
Meanwhile word comes that at last, by the emperor's order,
the holy bishop was returning from his unjust exile,
he with whom Martin had shared a glorious life
while the teacher of Poitiers flourished in his own land,
handing on the precepts of salvation to untamed peoples.
And though swift affection had quickly hurried the rejoicing saint away,
yet Hilary, impatient
of delay, had already left the lofty walls
of high Rome, to return more quickly to the land of Poitou.
So, following his footsteps on a devout course,
Martin gained his heart's desire and the end of his toil.
Here he builds a cell as a comfort for his weary limbs:
for his mind, full of God, dwelt in the heavenly seat.
Now if we were to recall here the songs of the ancient poets,
when sudden wonders shook their astonished senses,
their frenzied madness would cry out to wretched Phoebus
and would not let the false Muses rest even a moment;
the Delphic temples would be shaken by a lying Apollo,
and the whole throng of deaf sisters would be swept along,
or monsters stirred up would complete the frenzy:
but we, who seek our understanding and our words from Christ,
pray you, Martin, worshipper of Christ, to inspire us a little.
You who were able to give life back to the dead,
supported by the Lord's help, give health back to me:
I will be the first to show the miracle of life restored,
I will be the first to burst the bars of a stinking tomb.
Dead in my whole heart, I ask a just thing of my patron:
that a living mind may tell the glories of such praise.
So, though the lofty deeds surpass my powers of speech
and the measure of my eloquence cannot match their praises,
I will make the attempt. You, reader, whoever you are, who scorn such poor
verses: while you mock the words, you will marvel at the deeds.
A certain man, seeing the wonders of so famous a life,
chose to attach himself to so great a master,
though the mystic water of the font had not yet renewed him.
A fever, devouring all his marrow to the core,
wrung his frail life from his wasted body.
The teacher happened to be away at the time, but the brothers
in their devoted care were sorrowfully mourning the lifeless corpse,
grieving over their brother's punishment, not the death of his flesh.
The saint arrives and bathes his face with abundant tears,
pitying the dead man's sad fate, and he filled
the whole place with his cries. Soon, sending the witnesses away,
he burst into the cell, made mournful by so sad a death.
Then he threw himself upon his lifeless friend,
embraces the limbs that were cold in every part,
and breathes a faint breath over the stiffened face.
Yet his whole hope is placed entirely in the Lord:
he entreats the accustomed kindness, asks for the familiar
mercy, and by believing he earns the merit of faith.
The confidence of a pure heart saw that God was present,
and the body felt the effect of those holy breaths.
The prayer was not held in suspense for even two hours:
little by little the linen sheet moves as the limbs stir,
the dry limbs are watered by the moisture of the veins,
the icy breast grows warm with the breath of the soul,
and the clouded eyes are unsealed as light floods in.
Happy they who, at the dawning of the light restored,
were granted to see Martin first in the world!
Suddenly, with an effort, the whole body rises,
and the skin, long livid on the wasted limbs,
takes on a rosy glow from a healthier sap.
Easy voice, steady step, ready hand, vigorous heart:
the whole man, his body compounded of various elements,
received one single life in its diverse functions.
Soon the greatest joy calls forth a mighty shout:
the tongue sounds praises, herald of a grateful mind,
and the cry of the mouth proclaims the feeling of the heart.
Soon the crowd burst through the doors and filled the cell,
and a harmonious chorus sang the saint's praises.
And the man, to renew his life entirely after death,
at once shone, renewed by the eternal water,
and, blessed, lived on into old age for many years,
a witness for no short time to so famous a deed.
For he often used to tell many people
how he had trembled before the tribunal of the eternal Judge,
consigned to vile throngs and plunged in darkness,
until a prayer, uttered in angelic words,
offered the plea to the Lord and brought back his life.
This man was the first to make Martin known in our lands;
by this entrance his glory came to its further praises.
Not much time indeed had passed after these miracles
when new glory hastened on another famous deed.
For as he was passing the neighbouring estate of Lupicinus,
no humble or insignificant man, but one renowned almost throughout the world
for his worth, so that the glory might shine the more clearly,
confirmed by so great a witness,
drawing the unlearned common folk through so many miracles,
he heard from afar the cries of people weeping piteously
and stopped: he asks the cause and learns it in turn,
and just compassion stirred his devout grief.
For one servant, with a noose tightening on his throat,
had madly broken the bounds of his life and wrenched it away.
He runs up quickly and embraces the sad corpse,
the bulging eyes, the throat drained of blood,
the eyes too grim, and the face menacing in death.
Again there is weeping to the Lord, again sighs
and groans, the cry of the heart, the great voice of one silent:
the same faith of merit, and no lesser grace in the gift.
He is welcomed by a rejoicing chorus and a thronging crowd:
they display to all the miracles of Christ the Lord,
and the joys of a believing people, spoils won from the enemy.
BOOK TWO.
See, a new sea now opens wide, and kindly breezes
have drawn my leaking keel out into the midst of the waves,
and while the joys of a calm sea sweep me along,
my reckless little boat has broken out into the vast deep,
though it could barely skim the shores along the nearby lands.
What do I do now? Where, trembling, shall I steer my wavering prow?
The winds lure me onward; dread calls me back.
Let us press on, since land is far away, wherever the wave may draw us,
if only Martin's spirit will spread a gentle breeze
and grant the traveller a light wind, so
that the rotting sail may bear the favouring gusts.
Until now, while I told of the monk's way of life and deeds,
I kept to the shore; now the teaching of the bishop's chair will be my open sea.
Now I shall recount the glorious deeds of the great bishop.
Once there flourished greatly in the lands of the Gauls
the city of Tours, broad in its fields and teeming with people.
But longing to be made stronger still by such a bishop,
it burned with all its prayers to gain Martin.
But he drove all pride far from his holy heart,
and his humble mind stayed unmoved by their many entreaties,
until, with words contrived and tears forced out,
righteous lies overcame his excessive firmness.
For a certain man, aware of his great compassion, begged him,
lamenting the sad affliction of his ailing wife,
to deign in holy kindness to visit the one who pleaded with him:
by coming quickly he would be the cause either of her recovery
or of her death, if a harsh refusal delayed the answer to his prayers.
Sighs were joined to the feigned words,
and sobbing cries broken off into murmurs.
He kissed Martin's knees and clasped his feet in his arms,
outdoing true grief with so many fictions.
What wonder if a simple soul, a holy mind, follows the one who calls
when God compels it? For Martin himself
would rather have exposed the cunning scheme, had he not judged that this ought to be done.
As he came out, a crowd of people received him, doing him kindly
violence, and a great uprising of petitioners thronged the road,
a peaceful upheaval, a tumult without bitterness;
and an all-night guard even posted watchmen
on sentry and kept watch over its master, who was to be kept safe.
Their joys exulted in harmony, their prayers as one.
They went out to meet him; from every gate there rushed forth
eager zeal and the people's rival enthusiasm: all had one will,
and there was no division of mind in their zeal.
Some, however, were infected by devouring envy with the gall
of black poison, and, its goads searing the hearts of the wretches,
a carnal judgment drew them back to the opposing side.
Some, they even say (a thing wrong to believe), were bishops of learned
mind who were seized by a like madness,
mocking what ought to have gladdened them: that no elegance
had groomed his venerable face, that with his hair cut short
his open brow displayed the whole sign of the Lord,
and no cloud of quivering locks weighed upon his eyes;
that his shabby clothing, bearing witness to the brightness of his heart,
betrayed his zeal in prayer, because often, as he rolled his limbs
on the ground and lay pressed down with his body prostrate,
bristling dust had clung to his dirty fleece.
Rightly, then, so perverse a will gave way to the people,
and the sounder judgment of the common folk overcame the leading men.
For truly no one could be unaware of the judgment
of Christ who called him, proven by so many proofs.
Among the rest, whom a savage faction wanting the opposite
had wickedly gathered to itself, the most violent
was a bishop named Defensor: by that name, perhaps,
they thought the schemes of their false counsel
would be defended, though God, who approved what was just, refused.
For the devout people were celebrating the customary rite
in holy assembly, watching the mysteries in a crowded gathering,
while ever denser throngs packed around the altar
and his supporters in great numbers hung upon their hopes,
and the reader could not get past the obstacles in his way.
But a deacon who happened to be there, barely snatching up a book,
seized in the haste of the moment the very first verse
that the page of the psalm, hurriedly opened, had suddenly offered him,
and sang these words of the ancient prophet:
'Out of the mouth of infants, from the small murmur
of sucklings, you have made tender tongues pour forth praise
because of your enemies, so that this praise, uttered
by little ones, might destroy the perverse defender.'
A shout rose to heaven, and God's judgment was shown to be present,
God himself crying out: the sentence of Christ
overwhelmed the opposing side with a thunderbolt of words.
For that same verse approved the prayers of those who praised him
and checked the envious hearts of those who resisted.
Nor did the monk's labour grow any less thereafter, though his glory grew
by right of the priesthood. What must be done is taught by deeds:
the work of example persuades more than the charm of words.
So his clothing stayed the cheapest, his cloak worn thin;
so the precious modesty of his humble, holy heart remained;
so the blessed resolve of his unwavering life endured.
At first, then, he had a cell joined to the sacred
altars. Soon, so that his private prayer might escape
the thronging people and the constant crowds,
he went out and withdrew two miles from the city.
Nor was such nearness any harm to the remote cell:
a secluded lodging for the monk, a short road for the master,
a house near at hand for the teacher, far off for one seeking quiet.
On one side the edge of a naturally sheer rock,
the curving cliff, had enclosed it in a small hollow;
on the other the Loire, its banks bending in a gentle curve,
had fenced in the enclosed land with the barrier of its stream;
and a single narrow entrance lay open between the rock and the river,
where, a short way off along a confined path,
the flowing river touches the foot of the hill.
Here he chose to build a small cell from a pile of timber,
recognizing the mysteries of the holy wood,
the loftiest of guests entering beneath a humble roof,
so that the brothers who gathered there, schooled in modesty,
might learn to despise display through slender means,
vying to imitate the master who went before them by his example.
Others, though, did not care for wood: the nearby cliff, its hill hollowed out,
offered them recesses dug into the rock.
A just admiration had drawn eighty brothers there
to the mirror of such great virtue, so that from it
a blessed imitation might take the ways it beheld.
No one had anything of his own; all things were common
to all: love drew from a shared store.
No one was permitted to sell anything,
lest the shameless hunger for gold, once tasted, should grow.
He forbids them to practise a trade. One pursuit is allowed,
that of writing, which engages mind and eyes and hands
and holds them all together on a single point:
the gaze with sight, the heart with meaning, the right hand with order.
Yet only the young are kept to these tasks.
For to a mind already mature, prayer is enough,
so that one whose understanding the judgment of age has made firm
may strive for purity of heart and watchfully cleanse
the hidden inner eye, lest, veiled by the cloud of lurking
sin, it be deprived of the light of Christ.
No one went out freely: each was kept in his own
little cell. The company was given occasion to gather
only when the accustomed hour of prayer called them all together
and their harmony rendered praise to God from the heart,
or when, breaking the fast for their weary limbs,
they returned at a fixed time to the common tables,
so that the end of the day now spent, the flesh already tamed,
and the labour that followed in the night to be kept in vigil
might be divided by the very brief time of a frugal supper.
Only the sick, the rule relaxed for them, were permitted
to taste wine, so that the wasting of the ailing body
might be sustained by the scent of wine sprinkled in the cup.
Many wore clothing woven of camel's hair,
which pricked their wakeful limbs with light goads,
shutting out light sleep by stinging the flesh,
lest soft fleeces pamper a slack body
and wanton clothing flow in a fine cloak,
as the abundance of their former life had accustomed them.
For a wise resolve had drawn many there,
men famous for ancient lineage, to such a life.
All the more wonderful is it that after silken cushions and couches
this clothing and such rigour pleased those who entered.
In short, marvelling at the marks of such virtues,
neighbouring peoples and nearby towns
sought holy men from there as their rulers, vying with one another,
so that God's teaching, flowing from such a spring,
might spread watering streams into the hearts of the thirsty.
But now the time has come to touch at least a small part
of so vast a mass of mighty miracles.
And although disciples adorn the honours of true virtue,
and deeds should show beforehand what ought to be done,
yet I will touch on a very few of his own deeds,
showing his highest praises through brief signs.
There happened to be a tomb nearby which, often visited by worshippers,
vain superstition, falsely deceived, had consecrated
as a martyr's, forever paying it solemn honour.
Indeed, the bishops before him had even dedicated a venerable altar there,
so that the devotion might stand more firmly founded,
strengthened by the added rite of the sacraments.
But after Martin took up the reins laid upon him
and received the holy governance of the people entrusted to him,
he at once inquired into the name and titles of the venerated
martyr, and at what time he had earned the garlands
of so glorious a palm, or under what judge.
But when no record appeared that could reveal the truth,
and all antiquity refused to know of it,
he declined to believe such great things on doubtful words,
nor was the tale of a lying crowd enough for faith.
So he resolved, since the matter was doubtful and lacked the weight of witnesses,
to seek counsel from the Lord, before whom all times, ever subject to him,
stand present, though the ages have passed.
He hurried to the tomb with a few companions, so that through them
the miracles they witnessed might win belief from many.
So, when he had touched the mass of the sepulchre beside him,
there beside the cold ashes of dissolved flesh
his prayers went up to heaven: the traces of his flesh
are joined to the tomb, but his mind passes even beyond the stars.
Then he besought the Lord with all the power of faith
to reveal to those who did not know the merit and the name of the one buried there,
when suddenly, on his left, he saw a filthy shade,
which showed a black form with a sorrowful face
and displayed the most grievous fate of punished criminals,
confused and guilty, with a fearful look.
A voice too, uttered in the tearful words of one who mourns,
poured out its frequent sighs in such complaints as these:
'Let the old error cease to add torment to these pitiable shades
by bestowing on them a title not their own,
lest one for whom the punishment of his crime alone is enough
should see this burden grow, doubled by honour added to it.
And would that the saints, to whom this homage is rightly
paid, would deign to sprinkle with a tiny drop our
flames, the ceaseless burnings of the wretched!
They rejoice and enjoy everlasting light;
a horrid chaos has fenced us in with eternal darkness.
The confusion of night is far from the merits of light.'
This voice reached the ears of many far and wide,
but the form was revealed to Martin alone, whose
lighter mind passed beyond the weight of frail flesh,
piercing the bodily mass with the light of his heart.
At once the altar was removed, and all
the vain superstition that had counterfeited sacred rites was driven out.
The mysteries were transferred and passed over to true worship.
What, in the end, will be able to match these glories,
what art infected with magical tricks or stained with poisons,
weaving lying spells from contrived words
and probing stinking entrails, their veins inspected,
so that through the silences of hellish night it has sought out
a mad demon may bellow with deceitful murmur,
taking on a feigned face beneath a thin image?
Here surely a simple soul and nothing but the devotion of one who prayed
loosed the bonds of hell's law,
and though the limbs were pressed beneath the weight of the tomb,
yet the confession lived on in the present time.
Nor is this the end of his glories, nor do the garlands of his virtues
cease, broken off even for a short while.
For grace always clings to the saint as an inseparable companion
and is not confined within a fixed boundary of place.
It follows him when he goes out, stays undivided with him when he stays,
and, if there is reason for a journey, gladly goes with him on his way.
For while he was hurrying along the byways of the broad countryside,
where wild Gaul lies spread out in wide plains,
while a crowd of pagans followed a wretched corpse
and the linen shrouds, shaken, fluttered in the light breeze,
he, his gaze stretching far across the open plains,
thought the funeral procession was the worship of an unspeakable
demon, and that the bent necks of revellers were carrying
the rites of wretched cults to idolatrous images.
At once he raised the holy and venerable sign,
and, setting the cross against them, blocked them as they hurried on,
halting their unsteady steps by the weight of the banner.
Then indeed you could see the wretches held fast by the numbness laid on them,
their limbs grown stiff, their sinews bound,
their many efforts frustrated by their fettered limbs,
their steps halted, their pace frozen motionless,
the crowds shut in within a boundary set by command,
and the obstacles of a wall they could not climb
raising a vast barrier on every side,
until gradually, as he saw them more closely, it became clear
that a funeral honour was being carried. Then by that same
banner, by that very sign, their freedom was restored.
So by the command of the cross and the power of faith together
he had the right to bind the wanderers and to loose the bound.
I gather up these things touched on in haste, since the abundance
of his miracles urges me to treat praiseworthy deeds in brief sketches,
lest my paltry page, with long-winded words,
should delay minds hastening on to such great wonders;
and I am caught up once more by the weight of greater things.
Once he had cast down a sacrilegious temple, its roof overthrown,
levelling it to the ground, smashing the idols with the shattered beams
and crushing the images beneath the whole wreckage.
Near this place a broad pine
spread out its green boughs, and its aged arms, far and wide,
had woven a green forest in its leafy crown,
and with its lattice of leaves the dense grove of a single
tree kept off all heat: its perpetual shade
sheltered a constant mildness, a counterfeit spring.
This pine too he set about joining to the temple's ruins,
eager to roll into a like grave
whatever drew the hearts of the wretched into error.
Then indeed the senseless madness of the inflamed mob
strove to rush to the aid of the beloved tree
and to thwart his pious purpose with all its might.
Reason is no use to the mad, holy words no use to profane
minds, no more than a voice to the deaf or light to the blind.
He cried out that things could not bring salvation to man
which had no power for themselves; that the masters of wood
could not be helped by wood; that wood serves the bidding of the man
who chooses to be its servant, subject to what is subject to him, the same man
who picks from the forests some wood to burn and leaves some to revere.
Against this they shouted, wanting something very different,
their hearts deeply steeped in idolatrous poison:
'Stop trying to force the unwilling with long-winded words.
If you prove by deeds what you urge, this condition
will rightly satisfy us and win our belief: we ourselves will at once
set about cutting down our pine with all speed.
You, if you offer true proofs of your faith, as it falls
catch it, and gladly meet the ruin you desire,
trusting the Lord that you will suffer no harm.' So harsh a
bargain was accepted, and the most just of men did not refuse the unjust mouth,
trusting in the power of God, who could easily
have prevented the impending fall even by a word.
Without delay bonds were tied tightly around his limbs,
and, to be crushed, he was placed on that side
toward which the trunk leaned with its whole stem;
and now, its branches bending under their swaying weight,
it threatened the man beneath with the mass of a fall beyond doubt.
Their rival joys pressed on with all their hopes.
They kept at it with constant strokes and many axes.
Hope close at hand gave the weary courage and strength.
Revenge shut out pity, anger drove away pain.
The monks turned pale, half dead, and greater still was the danger
to a faith thrown into confusion by such terror,
until, gradually overcome by its wounds, the tree gave a crash
as it leaned, and, hurtling with a full plunge against the saint,
its speed outran the swift frenzy of their eager wishes,
its boughs already shattered, its whirling rush almost upon him.
He, with faith forbidding fear and dread driven away,
awaited the approaching fall with a steadfast heart,
lest unbelief, seeing the pine turned aside too soon,
should put the work down to chance and deny his merit,
taking it for a mere accident; but now, with the danger closer,
he raised his right hand, armed with the protection of the sign,
and set the cross against it. At once all its force
was broken, and, swiftly called back in a rapid turn,
the pine was carried the opposite way in a sudden whirl
against the authors of the crime. Those close by, who had been exulting,
trembled with fear at the ruin turned upon themselves:
those who had believed they had cautiously chosen a safe place
for so great a spectacle, scarcely recovering their wits,
saw their seats crushed by the shattered branches.
A shout rose to heaven, and the astonished surroundings
echoed, and voices rang out from the whole gathering:
the monks bore witness to their joy, the vanquished to the miracle.
Tongues sounded 'Christ', and with gracious lips at once
the ignorant and the knowing sang 'Christ': one party
acknowledged his favour, the other asked for faith. Thus in an instant a harmonious
will among those at odds, with Christ uniting them,
both earned the gift of faith and persuaded them to believe.
For surely there was no one at all in that crowd
who did not carry away the gifts of the salvation hoped for,
added to the Lord's flocks through the protection of the sign;
and places that reeked, beset with foul shrines,
mother Church soon covered with true temples.
Thus you conquer, Martin, thus you overwhelm your enemies,
thus your weighty sentence crushes those it overpowers: those
who were savage your merciful victory made brothers.
So the outcome sharpened his mind, and blessed victory
constantly fed his zeal for conquering the rebellious.
For scarcely were the idols smouldering in the dying flames,
and fine ashes still flying from the nearby fire,
when, on a similar temple, it kindled the burning anew,
that most just right hand, exulting in its many fires.
But while the whirlwind scattered the blazing heat far and wide,
and the fierce frenzy of the flames seethed in surging waves,
belching forth a swift cloud of fire,
swelling the fury gathered from the nearby destruction,
it attacked with its whole column a house not far off,
licking the neighbouring roofs with deadly flames.
When the saint saw in alarm that the danger was upon them,
and that the fire, now caught in the scorched beams,
had surrounded the house and engulfed it in a whirlpool of flames,
he hurried and climbed the roof with a swift leap,
where the fire pressed most densely on the house in a great mass,
and set his body in the path of the oncoming flames.
Then indeed the fires, bent back by a contrary blast,
turned into the wind, and although the gale pressed on,
the greater force of his command drove the flames back and compelled
the raging wind to give way to them at once.
So nature, overpowered, obeys the merits of the one who commands.
The flames are not driven by the gusts, but the gusts by the flames,
and the fire, following orders, did both things at once,
seizing what had been allotted to it, leaving what was defended.
So, when that temple had been vanquished by just fires,
he went on to destroy another, which the once wealthy village
of Levroux happened to worship with perverse mind.
But after the frenzied madness of the crowding mob
had driven back the work he attempted, and a whirlwind of violent
tumult had set all its fury against his undertaking,
he withdrew again to the remote seclusion of lonely places,
and there pressed on all the harder with holy prayers,
his earnest prayer continuing for three days
and joining to them as many hours of wakeful nights.
Moreover, clothed in a garment woven of hair,
he pricked his wasted limbs with its constant sharpness,
so that the harsh garment chafed his thin skin
and the skin, when touched, shrank from the bristling barbs;
he dashed himself on the stony ground, though his bones were harder still,
dragged out the slow days into late-ended fasts,
and drenched his whole face with a river of tears,
so that the ever-constant mercy of the Lord Christ,
taking deep pity on the toil of his innocent servant,
might grant success to his prayer and accomplish what he had attempted,
utterly removing the schemes of the opposing side.
Meanwhile he saw armed men standing near him
in angelic radiance, and recognition was not slow
to come: his face quickly regained its usual confidence,
and he was told in words besides the reason for their coming:
that he should not tremble, nor fear force, nor dread weapons,
recognizing through such signs that favour was at hand;
whatever crowd might rise against him in hostile tumult,
God's help was enough, who could at once
defeat all their hosts by the power of his word;
they themselves were bringing him help and carrying out God's commands.
So, his spirit keener and his strength wholly regained,
believing these arms of the two sufficient for the war,
he returned in strength to the work he had begun, and into the midst of the throngs
burst the constancy restored to his trembling heart.
The temples were laid low, utterly overthrown in ruins:
the images lay fallen beneath the whole mass,
and the broken idols sank under the toppled roofs.
A mingled dust enveloped everything together at once:
beams, altars, statues, mortar, stones, metal.
Nor indeed did anyone from that great crowd step forward
to confront him. He stood undaunted,
seeing the hearts of the trembling men subdued.
The people waited, motionless. The breasts of those who had threatened
grew stiff, and their hearts were stunned, their inmost parts dazed.
Their limbs could make no movement, their words no uproar:
the wretches' limbs went rigid, the voice stuck in their throats,
the hands of those who tried fell slack, and so did the shouting of those who gaped.
As the sea, stirred up from its lowest depths
by the whirlwind of a violent storm bearing down on the waves,
dashes against all the crags with foaming spray
and with hoarse roar overleaps the banks that stand in its way,
while the broken masses of water pound the hollow shores
and the nearby shallows are mingled with the whole deep;
then soon, when the winds have fallen silent and their motion ceased,
a vast plain of calm waters is spread out,
the smooth marble surface settles as the wind dies down,
and the element lies motionless, its face transformed,
tempting slight skiffs across its levelled flood:
just so the madness of the raging mob fell silent,
laid its storm to rest and let its blasts subside,
and, submissive to true words, shouted this alone:
that Martin's Lord must be worshipped throughout the whole world,
that they knew him alone as God. For if deaf
idols could ever bestow salvation on one who asked,
they would bring it to themselves; and no one can give a gift
he lacks: whoever begs from the needy is the poorer.
So, having fully received the splendour of the true light,
this crowd too was added, in devotion, to the camp of the faithful.
His heart constantly invigorated by such triumphs,
he longed for wars again: increased faith removed alarm,
hope of merit gave him spirit, the dread of danger gave way.
For soon a similar cause stirred up a similar tumult,
when, to rescue a temple from being overthrown, there hurried
a peasantry beyond all reason mad, swelling its usual stubbornness
with the vast weight of headlong fury.
In short, madness had so overwhelmed all their sense
that one man ran up, threatening him with drawn sword,
daring to brandish sacrilegious steel to wound him.
And when the saint, throwing back his covering, gladly
offered his bared neck, the man, not drawing back in the least,
rose in fury over his sword raised high.
Higher still he lifted his mad right hand aloft,
raising his whole body with a swift effort,
straining his hurried steps in a headlong lunge,
so that the blow, coming from higher, might fall more fiercely:
when suddenly his body went rigid, his sinews tightened,
and the movement stuck fast, spent in thin air,
and his outstretched right hand held the steel suspended, useless,
and the whole blow died away in his numbed limbs,
and his hand remained fixed, its effort mocked.
Then his limbs, collapsing backward with all their weight,
crashed headlong to the ground,
and his bones rang out as his battered limbs were crushed,
and lay prostrate on the stony heap of earth.
Then at last groans were wrung from him and tears forced out,
and, his threats laid aside, the most pitiable entreaty
of the suppliant turned to seek saving pardon.
Why, I ask, did you call back your right hand from the blood it craved?
Why do you spare one whom no one asks you to spare? What holds back
your blow, if your anger remains? Surely you do not wish to forgive:
why hold back the steel? See, the innocent neck lies open,
bared to your wounds: why delay your wishes,
you who have the mind of one who strikes? Why, while the crime stands,
is vengeance put off? Even if your right hand stops, you are doing
what you long to have done. If the will is not changed,
the guilt remains: the heart's intent is enough to decide desert.
Nor indeed was this the only time the gifts of life preserved
were seen by the trembling hearts of the astonished people.
For soon after, when a like madness was about to inflict a like death
with drawn weapon, suddenly the blade was struck away
and deserted the striker, his blow falling in vain;
his frenzied right hand groped for the weapon wrenched from it,
and his cheated eyes, the steel now lost, saw all the aims
of his pent-up fury melt away.
Yet at times he was accustomed to persuade by wholesome counsel,
to change fierce minds with words,
and to soften hardened hearts with holy speech,
lighting up the ancient night with the light of doctrine.
Moreover, it was easy for him to restore health
to the sick, the power to walk to the lame, and sight to the blind.
For surely no disease, however violent,
had so overwhelmed anyone that he did not regain the comforts of the health he longed for,
rejoicing to grow strong again at the sight of the saint.
This may be made plain even by the present deed.
Once, within the walls of Trier, an unmarried maiden
had wasted away, consumed by grievous paralysis,
and her numbed limbs lacked all motion,
deprived of their proper functions. Already, as the flesh failed,
only a faint breath stirred in her chilling breast.
Her kin grew pale with fear as death drew near
and watered her withered limbs with a fountain of tears,
and a mournful throng of attendants had already been gathered
by the sad honour soon to be paid at her funeral, when, breaking in on the murmurs of the mourners,
a messenger rushed in, crying out
that Martin had come, who was readily able
to grant the longed-for cure by his holy prayers.
As soon as this word reached the father's sorrowing ears,
he rushes off, half-dead, and throws himself at the saint's knees, begging
for help, and bathes his footprints with copious weeping;
sobbing sighs break off his words,
and his tears say more of his prayers than his words do.
But the saint, strong in modest piety,
shares his feeling but disclaims the merit. He denies that he has
the power to give help, yet in his heart he shares
the grief. He shuns display, but weeps over the distress,
and proves his merit by avoiding it. Thus he stands the loftier
for his humble heart; what he takes from honour he adds to praise.
Seeing this, the father presses all the more vehemently,
until, moved by persistent and just entreaty,
the holy urging of the priests, joined to the father's prayers,
compelled him, though he refused, by gentle right
to visit the mournful inner rooms of the grieving parent.
The people stand before the doors; the miracles of Christ
are awaited by the hearts of the astonished crowd, hanging in suspense.
When, moved with pity, he saw the half-dead girl's wasted
limbs and her eyes languishing from consuming ills,
the skin clinging to the bones of her dried-up body,
the colour of her skin tainted by suffused bile,
and, with even the murmur of her tightly bound tongue gone,
a slight breath drawn from her icy breast,
and the threads of her veins dying as the pulse broke off,
its rhythm cut short, ready to leave her wrist,
at once he lays himself on the ground, his whole body prostrate,
asking the Lord for the medicine of the Word,
for whom it is enough to command, and to overcome all art with a nod.
He sensed that God was present. He asks for oil to be brought out.
A holy blessing is added to the liquid offered him.
Then, rejoicing in the anointing of the transformed juice,
he touches each limb with the healing chrism.
His holy right hand, laid on her, drives out the long-standing pain,
and the happy gifts of the health obtained by prayer
gradually flow back, poured in at the healer's touch.
Thus, with diseases put to flight from every part of the limbs,
strength returns and takes their place in the revived body.
Soon the girl rises up strong, as the people marvel,
and, planting firm steps by the divine gift,
gives praise to Christ the Lord at the holy altars.
After this work of power had filled the city, thronged with gatherings,
all came running, vying with one another,
whose minds a demon or whose bodies disease
had overwhelmed, begging a cure for heart and limbs.
Some went away steady on their feet, others sound in mind.
Yet above all the miracles which the grace of Christ
deigned to work through its servant,
the immediate cure of one slave stood out,
whom a demon held captive in full possession.
In short, when the saint, moved by the great urging of those who asked,
ordered the wretch to be brought to the holy
threshold, no one could bind the raging man.
So, raving with rabid mouth, he put everyone to flight,
gnashing his teeth; blood had covered his torn body all over,
and wounds stood out horribly on his naked limbs.
Then his master, exalted to a very illustrious rank,
adorned with the fasces of a proconsul, forgetting this
dignity, comes and throws himself at the kindly knees,
and, prostrate at his feet, wraps his arms around them in supplication,
begging that, since neither force nor chains availed
to drag along the servant raving with maddened heart,
he himself would come to the house where for a long time now
a constant guard had kept the slave shut up.
But the saint refused to tread the threshold of a pagan,
nor would the righteous man go under idolatrous rafters,
setting the stench of the temple apart from the chrism of Christ.
But the man, clinging forcefully to the holy knees,
promises that, if his servant were healed, he would be willing to believe
whatever the teaching of so great a master should hand down.
Then at last, moved by so just a plea from the petitioner,
he brought his longed-for steps to the threshold that was to be saved,
and the same medicine brought help to the master, who asked so justly,
as to the servant. Both rejoice,
the one glad at faith received, the other at his mind restored.
And straight after these miracles a new deed
roused the astonished people to still greater praises.
For, happening to enter the doorway of a neighbouring house,
he cries out that he sees, right in the doorway,
the foul shade of a raging demon, horrible to behold.
Without delay the enemy, now exposed, at once began
to rage, seizing the cook, to throw into tumult
the innermost rooms of the house, to gnash his jaws,
and to bare the menacing teeth of the captive mouth,
venting his inborn wrath through another's bites,
while the demon's madness, mingled with the man's, shakes the possessed body,
so that its rage raves through a human mouth,
armed for its own frenzies with another's teeth.
They scatter in fear, and no one dares to resist,
and what they see sharpens their fear to the utmost.
But the saint, trusting in the Lord, laughs at the scattering
crowd, and with swift approach places himself in the demon's path.
Indeed, while madness was shaking the quivering jaws,
clashing the wretched teeth with a savage growl,
and snapping again and again with tossing head,
he steadfastly thrust his fingers into the gaping throat,
halting the savage dominion of the hostile robber.
The greedy jaws stuck fast, the bite withheld;
the shameless fury of the open mouth froze, suspended;
the tongue beneath rejoiced at the healing touch,
and gentle kisses pressed the hand thrust in.
Then, since no escape lay open through the blocked mouth,
the demon, expelled in a flux of the belly, left the bowels emptied
and took nothing from the body but a stench.
Meanwhile the whole city was suddenly thrown into
turmoil. A wicked rumour reported barbarian movements,
spreading countless fears through credulous hearts.
Yet no bearer of this report could be found,
so that the tale might be confirmed by a known source.
So when he saw such fires stirred up over such doubtful matters
and the people gripped by vague terror,
he commanded the demon shut up in a captive body
to reveal where the tale had come from that spread this new rumour.
At once, driven to confess by the word as by a torturer,
he cries out that he is the cause, the crime and the source of the evils:
that he, with his fellow spectres, had sown these lies
to crush the trembling people with fear.
So this true confession of the lying robber
set the anxious minds free, while the demon was tormented.
But to recount the deeds of such great goodness,
neither my barren mind nor my poor page will suffice.
O truly kindred virtues, ready compassion
and a humble mind! He who loves all scorns no one.
For vile leprosy had covered a certain man with its dreadful disease,
staining all his flesh with a covering of spots
and scattering dense sores over his corrupted body.
While the frequent disgust of the healthy marked him out,
and their most unjust minds, ignorant of their own lot,
despised the sad disease in another's body,
the saint, entering the gate with a crowd going before him,
such as had gathered to attend so great a patron
and was packing the city gateway in dense throngs,
gives kisses to the wretch, joining face and mouth with his,
and, not fearing that his face would be defiled by such a touch,
pressed the seal of peace upon lips joined to his own.
The others were stunned. But the man, rejoicing,
felt in that touch the bounty of the divine gift,
and swift health returning quickly through his limbs,
and a quick radiance spreading through his renewed flesh.
O truly precious the condescension of your peace,
and the medicine that ever flows from your holy mouth!
Whether you touch limbs with your lips or hearts with your speech,
your kisses will heal the sick, and your words those who need teaching.
And would that a like mercy might touch our own diseases,
and that Martin would be willing to drive away the stains of a wretched heart
by praying with so holy a mouth!
Then, I believe, I would be called back to the joys of true peace,
lifting my healed face to the holy mysteries,
and after squandering the wealth my portion had given me —
my hope hanging on the lips of a merciful Lord —
leaving the food of swine and the pleasures of the flesh,
I would receive the sure seals of true faith.
Indeed, even the mere touch of his garment, or its fringe,
and threads snatched eagerly from his torn cloak
brought swift cures in every case.
For, to pass over deeds done no less openly
for humble folk that have remained unknown, will, I ask, he remain unknown —
Arborius, who held the world's highest honour,
who, renowned at the summit of the lofty prefecture,
governed Rome with the reins entrusted to him,
and was no less outstanding in uprightness of pious character?
His only daughter, wasting away, her limbs utterly consumed,
had laid her feeble frame back upon her bed —
a daughter whom a fever, by the fixed law of its recurrence
returning every fourth day, had so stripped of the clothing of flesh
by ever repeating its frequent assaults
that her afflicted body could feel no relief
even on the days between, so close was the fever,
since the tossing just past claimed one of them,
and on the other she suffered in dread the onslaught to come.
So while her father nursed the girl in this state with sorrowing love,
and while over her icy limbs, with its warm breath,
the frequent panting of the father's mouth passed,
a letter was delivered into his trembling hand,
which the holy bishop was sending to his grieving friend.
When, rejoicing at the gift of the page, he had read it through
and joyfully pressed kisses on the absent man's hand,
with a swift motion he rolled up the venerable letter
and hastily laid it on her panting breast.
O truly precious faith! The fever is driven off and put to flight,
and the flame of its fiery heat is taken away.
The blessing, present there, penetrates the parched veins
and waters the exhausted marrow with the dew of words,
restoring swift health by the Lord's loving-kindness;
to whose praise we shall rightly and joyfully ascribe
what we now marvel that faithful servants could do.
Nor did this medicine bring healing to the limbs alone,
but faith, now increased, added true salvation for the heart.
For at once the maiden, vowed to God, is offered to the Lord through him
through whom, rescued from disease, she had been made well.
Thus the grace of this gift was granted to three at once:
the bishop consecrates, the father offers, the maiden is consecrated.
Indeed a like medicine restored health to Paulinus too,
whom the glory of his outstanding faith has exalted far and wide.
His sight then lay hidden beneath a cloud drawn over it,
and a fog, spread out with darkness poured in,
shut out all light with a covering of spots.
This a light sponge, held with a gentle touch, put to flight,
with the blessing of his right hand close at hand,
scarcely touching the eye. His sight, now restored, learned
to bear the light, and in wonder received a new brightness.
And would that the medicine of our holy patron might be willing
to touch the darkness of our heart with such a light,
so that the mysteries of that former deed might be renewed,
with the same name, the same physician, and a like cause for healing.
We marvel indeed, seeing so many great
remedies of the holy chief physician; let us marvel too at the
cure that the physician himself earned, with Christ as his physician,
through whom the good man, at once generous and grateful for a gift,
rejoices in gifts both given away and kept.
For, as he was striving to climb to an upper part
where the house rose high, supported on lofty columns,
while he set his feet on the slippery stairs, he pitched
headlong, and, tumbling again and again down the steps,
fell and struck the ground with his body crushed.
But lo, while his broken, exhausted limbs groaned
with fierce pain, bringing sudden comfort to the afflicted man
an angel stands by him, venerable with holy countenance,
hastening to wash his wounds with water poured over them,
gently touching them with the ointment of an unknown balm,
spreading the thin liquid with a light touch.
From this the moistened limbs quickly felt a swift cure,
as his body was soothed and his veins were refreshed,
and at once his limbs grew strong and steady; the pains,
routed on every side, departed at the Lord's command.
Swift steps, a lively mind, joy of heart and mouth,
a face in harmony with a grateful breast.
While he praises the Lord, he claims nothing for himself from it,
and revealed his merit by denying that he had merited it.
BOOK THREE
Why, barren reed, do you call forth again a voice
sent hissing from cracked stalks? This glory surely
deserves to be magnified by the voices of greater trumpets,
nor can a voice burst from little reeds as great
as one that could fill even lofty clarions.
But if so narrow a pipe is helped by even a slender breath,
one sent by the blessing of a holy mouth,
then though it cannot utter grand things, it will at least speak sweet ones.
The first part of the book, then, will belong to ambition overcome.
This door will unlock the remaining praises:
through it, after many ages of degenerate fear,
lost freedom shone forth in a corrupted world.
Once, elated by wars successfully waged,
Maximus, already proud at the death of one lord
and the exile of another, had by his success aggravated the crime that clung so ill to his character,
and the wounds of his depraved nature
had often been torn open again by prosperity, the more ill-starred in a proud heart,
prosperity bound to fall all the harder amid good fortune.
To this king, then, from different quarters, many
shepherds of God came, whose constant care it is
to protect or to feed the Lord's devout people,
striving to release the accused and to free those in chains,
to give rest to the weary and comfort to the sorrowful,
to beg a homeland for exiles and to pray for pardon,
to win for the wretched proscribed their property and their lives.
And while they labored with kindly zeal to speed these things,
little by little, bowing with trembling assent to the swollen man,
the holy dignity of the fathers began to grow far too cheap,
given over to flatteries, not such as the ancient dignity
of priests was wont to pay, but such as the foul ambition of clients pays,
cast down at the nod of an arrogant patron.
Among them Martin alone, steadfast in heart and speech,
stained his devout heart with no false color,
nor did trembling cowardice smother with an ugly blemish
a mind humble before Christ, but lofty toward the heights of the world.
Indeed, standing firm even in his very requests,
if ever there was cause to petition the swollen king,
he made his petition as though he had the right to command.
Often, too, the king's ambition assailed the holy man
with repeated entreaty, that he might come at last,
so often invited, to the king's spurned banquets.
For he, scorning pride and pondering the man's deeds,
utterly refused to join himself to the table
of one whose crimes he thought it a sin to link
with his holy mind by even the slightest assent,
casting in his face the slaying of his lords and an empire
won by blood, the death of a king and the reign of a tyrant.
But the king, wearying that devout heart with continual entreaties,
sought to wash away his guilt, and, clearing himself of the crimes charged,
said that the rule of the empire had been imposed on him
by the terror of those who commanded it; that it was wrong for power
wrested from him by sword and arms to be crushed beneath a weight of odium
when it was free of ambition; that no small signs
of His favor had the Lord sent in so great a triumph,
nor was anyone, however lukewarm and slight his faith,
unaware that the fortunes of war
hang upon the nod of God; and that it was plainer still,
when the side inferior in valor and men defeats one trusting more in numbers,
that the victor has won by the judgment of Christ;
nor indeed had he done anything bloody, even after the wars,
with a pitiless spirit, and the fury of the sword
had had no force after the battle; after arms and trumpets
the guiltless swords had ceased from the crime of slaughter,
and the peace was spattered with no blood at all.
Repeating such things often and pleading ever more urgently,
he softened the holy man's rigor by repeated argument,
so that, pardoning the fault and won over by his zeal, Martin went
to the dishes of the royal table he had formerly disdained.
Hope, now nearer fulfilment, exults at so great a boon.
The festal day rejoices to shine with a happy gathering.
Chosen nobles are added, those whom the splendor of an office
close to the royal summit binds to it,
distinguished by robes of state, holding authority over laws and arms,
the rights of the forum or the trumpets of war.
Among these, in the middle, where the couch bends in its curve,
the priest reclined. On right and left the rank of powerful
commanders, their limbs laid on golden couch-frames,
pressed the purple of precious fleece spread beneath them.
At the king's right hand, venerable with holy countenance,
sat the old man, like Moses when, bringing back the sacred laws,
he came down from the holy summit of the mountain,
flashing with the exceeding brightness of his transformed face,
when the splendor of his countenance displayed the face of his heart
and no veils could contain the new light.
The attendants, a rejoicing throng, marvel in silence,
and the devoted court vies in modest services
to wait on so holy a man. All have one care,
the duty they longed for; reverence for the king counts for less.
The king himself, though present, prefers that Martin should take precedence.
Royal dishes crowd the tables set below;
rich purple gleams on the lofty couches;
soft silks dyed crimson stir and sway,
and there glows, in skilfully drawn threads that hold no wool,
softened metal spun into thread and woven with the purple.
Hangings stretched across the proud thresholds tremble,
and at the doors the movable barrier of curtains sways.
Everything gleams with varied adornment, above and below:
the walls with paintings, the floors with marble, the ceilings with metal.
Capacious crystal holds glassy waters,
and since it looks like both the vessel and the water,
you would not think that any barrier held the liquid poured in.
Cups are poured from jewels, and from jewels drunk;
masses of electrum set off the tawny gold.
The craftsmanship was prized, yet the material was more precious than the craft.
Some vessels glitter with gems, some stand out with figures in relief;
some are rough to the eye but smooth to the touch.
On gleaming platters and wide dishes are set
the fruits of air and woodland, of land and sea.
When hunger had been banished by the feast, the only wish
was to relieve parching thirst. The servants snatched up
ice enclosed in gold and snow-cold waters;
others offered dewy bowls. The care and briskness
of the servants anticipate the wish of those who ask.
Then the king commands the hesitant servant to offer it to Martin,
yielding him the honor, and at the same time, reversing the order,
ardently longing to take the cup after so holy a hand,
so that the bowl, made more precious by the touch of such lips,
might steep the liquid poured into it with heavenly dew.
But scarcely the slenderest drop of wine wetted him;
it vanished on lips barely moistened by its touch.
When the king stretched out his hand to take the cup,
Martin, weighing the honor due to faith, handed it to his own
priest. The merit of the heart, not the king's purple,
prevailed; the diadem gave way to the faith he preferred.
The hearts of the men who watched stood transfixed, their minds stunned,
and his steadfastness, even with the king slighted,
pleased more than it astonished; nor did the spite
of envy scorch the king as he weighed the import of so great a deed.
What priest, however great, even before a petty judge,
would dare so much for holy right?
Terror did not overcome the firm man, nor favor the just one,
nor the eagerness of his host, nor the anger of the mighty.
O virtue near to God! Thus, with the heart withdrawn,
to be as though far off yourself, and to conquer the world while present in it!
Nor did he fear to declare boldly to the king himself
whatever the kindly Spirit had revealed to him, filling
his devout heart with the gift poured in, things not to be doubted:
the changing fortunes of war, first battles
successful, then soon a grievous defeat in another conflict.
As his fiery mind saw all these things with pure perception,
so swift events proved his words, as though he had seen them happen.
For in the first contest Maximus routed and crushed the king,
but soon bowed his captive neck to the returning commander.
Nor is it a wonder that so keen a mind saw so much,
leaving all cares behind with lofty heart
and soaring with heavenly perception far above the stars.
For often the faithful monks standing before his doors
were amazed to hear him mingling his words with the speech of angels.
Thus his body and perishable limbs felt nothing of the body,
and to a mind already enjoying freedom
the weight of the subdued flesh did no harm at all.
The demon too, whatever face he assumed to deceive him,
lay plainly exposed, his efforts in vain,
and was not allowed to play his games with changing shapes.
At last, when no escape at all lay open to the trembling fiend,
he would breathe out his savage venom in raging words,
seeking to inflame with speech the man his snares could not harm,
to tear with the poison of his tongue the one who had slipped from his teeth,
pouring out his empty anger, his efforts already broken.
Once, indeed, shaking a right hand dripping with pitiful blood
and displaying the evidence of a killing on a bloody horn,
glad at evil and laughing at sorrow,
he burst into the holy cell with a deadly muttering,
pouring out his hellish voice in insolent words:
'See,' he said, 'the proof that my fury has at last been fulfilled.
Chance gave me these weapons; this weapon I drove violently home,
winning through the service of a beast, but by our crime.
And, what makes the fruit of the crime the greater, he was yours, one of your
own band, who has fallen to solace our wrath,
renewing my exhausted strength with the blood I longed for.'
At once Martin summons the senior brothers and bids them all
hurry with anxious concern to visit the monks' cells,
lest perhaps the lying words of the deceitful brigand
had for once told the truth about his own crime,
as the voice of sorrowful defendants is wont to do
when under a cruel torturer they confess deeds that merit punishment.
Then they report that none at all of the brothers
bore the mark he spoke of; they had counted before them the whole
flock of the saints, which, shut within the fold,
scorned the rage of the wolves gnashing at the gates,
the flock that watchful Martin nourished for the eternal King.
Yet one man, hired for wages, had gone out
to bring wood by wagon to ward off the cold.
Martin orders them to hurry to meet him, believing
that this man, made a companion of the monks if only by his employment,
had lain open to the snares of the self-confessed brigand.
Without delay the guess is proved true on the spot.
Going out, they see, not far from the threshold, half-dead,
the poor man breathing out the last breaths of life.
Yet he, opening his eyes that drooped in death,
with the broken murmur of a tongue scarcely able to sob,
drew a faint voice from his icy breast,
explaining the cause of his wound. For by chance an ox,
while its loosened yoke-bands were being bound tight with straps,
its neck too free and wandering, rebellious against its master,
had pierced his soft groin with a hellish horn.
When he had told this and fell silent, his lips pressed shut,
he laid down his weary head in death, and over face and limbs
a saffron pallor spread across his icy body.
So he died. Yet for us this end too
revealed the merit of Martin, to whom it was granted
so to know the future that the veils of the flesh
in no way slowed his swift mind with their earthly weight.
In vain the enemy, utterly lying and cunning,
tried to hide his frauds in ambush or deceive with shapes,
wasting these efforts so often to no purpose,
daring to mimic the forms of invented gods
and to feign the likeness of those whose honor was itself a fiction:
now the incestuous face of Jupiter and the fury of Mars,
Mercury with false wings bound to his feet,
Vulcan with his tongs, or Phoebus with strings and plectrum
he portrayed, Minerva frenzied with shield and crest,
wanton Venus, Diana beating the coverts,
the sister wed by an unlawful law of marriage,
who lost the name of sister through her brother's crime.
Displaying himself in such shapes, deeds worthy of his own kind,
and betraying his own crimes by the face he feigned,
he could not slip away; his fraud uncovered,
the demon, mocked, lost his cunning efforts,
breathing out his last venom in insolent words
and assailing the unharmed man with abuse and outcry.
All this Martin's patience bore with unmoved face,
scorning flattery, laughing at insults and reproaches,
and, recognizing the deceitful enemy in either fiction,
he could neither be hurt by accusation nor moved by praise,
setting the signs of salvation against the darts of words
and shattering the brigand's weapons by holding up the cross.
Often assailing that devout heart with harsh complaints,
the impious one dared, alas, to reproach the pious man
for his love of mercy, shouting so loudly before him
that his deadly words were heard plainly by many witnesses.
'Why,' he said, 'if you condemn crimes, do you receive
those hateful to the Lord, and, while blaming vice, seek the company
of sinners? Perhaps the deeds of your men are hidden from you,
done back then at my urging, many of which I persuaded them to,
and in which I had a large share. Who, I ask, will approve
a man hostile to deeds but indulgent to those who do them?'
Martin said: 'Serpent swollen with ancient venom,
this is not the judgment of Christ the Lord concerning the wretched,
who, if he sees guilt brought to an end, lays aside his anger,
setting no term for punishment save the term of the offense,
warning that sins must not continue, forgiving those that have ended,
gentle toward the past if there is amendment now,
calling back the erring, pardoning the crimes of those called back,
patient with the perverse, merciful and gentle to those who return:
life of men, death of sins; compassionate in both,
he bids the destruction of sin become the cause of salvation.
Nor would I despair, trusting in his proven goodness,
that even though your crimes surpass all offenses,
you without whom no one commits any wickedness, and who in all
[?] are mingled with their sins and rightly [?] mingled in their punishments,
if you would grieve for what you have done, however long ago, even at this late hour,
mercy would snatch you from the midst of the flames.'
O blessed devotion, that anyone should trust so much
in the goodness of the Lord God as to dare to promise kindly
even what he admits has not been promised,
while he tries to call back from his accustomed crime
the very author of crime, removing sin from its kindling
and cutting off the hateful stock at its first root!
But since our murmurs, striving to sing of frequent triumphs,
have touched upon the tyrant of hell,
and since, wishing to recount amid the titles of praise
the series of battles, we have sounded the enemy's name,
we will tell in our discourse this too, which Christ has granted,
a deed done at that time which we greatly marvel at.
Once there was a young man, joined to the companions of the saints and ministers of Christ,
bright in deed as in name, called Clarus,
who had set up his cell not far from the holy teacher,
gathering many brothers into a righteous fellowship,
so that a harmony might sing in tuneful, devout hymns
