and glory resound in concord from united tongues.
A certain crafty young man, carrying feigned
pretenses and contrived wiles, and counterfeiting every
appearance of innocence, deceiving under the name of monk,
sought him out in sheep's clothing but with the mind of a wolf,
breathing the ancient venom from his corrupted breast.
And at first, mingling with the saints in body alone,
the pretender put on a show of the common life.
Afterwards, wont to boast of conversations with angels,
he had lifted his deceitful mind to vain heights,
destined to fall all the further from the summit of his elated heart.
Indeed, persuading by wonders, he drove unwary
hearts, as though his merits were already proved by evidence,
to trust his swollen words on the strength of trifling signs.
At times he would boast of conversing
with the Lord himself, as though a messenger
constantly brought him word from the heavenly throne,
showing him great favor in familiar talk.
Nor did he fear to compare himself with the holy prophets,
breathing the lying words of the deceitful brigand.
And by now he had driven many to believe his invented
words. Clarus alone, with steadfast heart,
repelled the deceitful murmurs from his holy mind,
and though the madman feigned the Lord's anger,
he could neither frighten the grave man nor deceive the wary one,
though he promised that his power would be proved by many signs.
For, so that miracles might ensnare deceived minds,
he sought to confound his astonished hearers with words like these:
'This night,' he said, 'God, lest the grace be thought vain
which he has willed to decree for our merits,
will clothe me in a fleecy garment white as snow.
When these gifts lie plainly before your eyes,
then at least, if you hesitate to believe my words, believe
what you see, and readily praise the favor you behold.'
Then indeed all waited, wakeful, for so great a portent,
to see how the promised marvel would turn out.
And behold, at about the hour of midnight,
when the night, dividing them, looks on either day not far off,
near to the one coming and not far removed from the one left behind,
the earth shook and trembled; a vast crash on every side
thundered horribly, and a fire more hideous than the darkness
flashed with a terrible torch and a counterfeit light.
Their trembling hearts are terrified by the sudden sight.
At once, then, eager and made bolder by his very success,
since the promised fraud had gone forward so far,
he gave the fleece to someone to touch and see.
That man quickly summoned the rest, so that the novel shape of the contrived trick
should not deceive one man alone. Those summoned marveled
up close at the garment, remarkable for its whiteness and its purple,
and at the weave yielding softly to their anxious hands
as they ran them over the soft threads of the fine web.
Yet no one could tell from what fleece it was spun,
though the robe shone close beside them, brought near;
but the garment, seen by the eye and believed by the touch,
kept its assumed shape, lying to both.
Then Clarus urged them all with wholesome exhortation
that, since things were thrown into such confusion by huge portents,
they should turn back to the Lord in prayer, for he alone
could expose hidden wiles and drag the brigand's fraud
out of its own darkness. Swiftly the whole wakeful
throng hastens to the sweet melodies of the accustomed psalms
and seeks comfort in holy hymns,
to drive off sluggish sleep with bodies refreshed
and conquer the night's silence with sacred songs.
Tears follow the psalms, sighs follow the voice;
the heart cries out if the tongue is silent; the whole time
is bound together in praise of the Lord, mind and mouth taking turns.
Meanwhile, as soon as they see the darkness of night thinning
as daylight draws near, when dawn, going before,
announces the sun, scattering the blush she has received from it
and veiling the wandering stars in saffron hue,
they seize the man and strive to bring him to the cell of holy
Martin, so that at last, the cloud dispersed, the demon, put to flight,
might lose the fictions of his deceitful wit,
his fraud laid bare before so great a judge.
But he, resisting, as the danger drew ever closer,
struggled to refuse and to escape the holy hands that held him,
planting his feet and resisting with his voice,
crying out that he was forbidden to approach the cell of holy
Martin or to carry that garment to his threshold.
Then indeed they press on: his trembling betrays the fraud,
and his pale cowardice lays bare the contrived wiles.
The phantom garment vanished in the hands of those who held him,
and the apparition melted away, leaving their eyes staring:
just as the fleecy mists, whose airy threads
have woven over the hollow valleys a counterfeit flood,
when the bright sun lifts his pure orb higher,
reveal the plains laid bare as the darkness scatters.
Fix this trophy too, holy Martin, to the cross,
by which you strip the savage tyrant of his feigned garment,
tearing apart the lying coverings of an airy web
and scattering the floating fleeces of a hollow cloud.
O fury that will never yield, do you rise again,
so often crushed? So often losing your efforts,
you rush in and fall, and your daring sets no limit,
nor does success fulfil your wish? Do you, impious one, counterfeit
the face of the Lord, and try to deceive the light with darkness,
so that by such an appearance your senseless madness
might delude the saint with contrived shapes,
breathing out your last venom, though it wounds no one,
and puffing out exhausted rage from jaws now empty?
You cannot pierce a pure mind with foul gloom,
nor can the shadows of clouds shut out the true sun;
and though, radiant in purple and flashing with gems,
you set ruddy gold beneath your lying feet,
feigning to be the true King with a false diadem,
proclaiming yourself, alas, faithless one, the eternal Christ,
so that impiety, veiled under a holy name and pretending to be God,
might perhaps lie hidden and persuade the blessed man
to believe in an enemy under the lying guise of deity
and to bend his devout limbs in honor of a demon,
so that a misplaced religion might make the saint, oh horror,
a sacrilegious man, and by believing he might lose the merits of faith,
and the deceitful cups of poison, wickedly offered,
might hide their dreadful juice in the sweetness of honey.
Spread these nets for ignorant minds; contrive these
snares for raw recruits, who with untried weapons
attempt the first prelude to the trumpets of war.
But one who is no novice, accustomed to sweat under arms
and to enclose victorious standards behind a rampart thrown up before them,
who covers his veteran grey hair with a venerable helmet,
who, taught by long practice, has foreseen everything,
anxiously scouting which places are safe for laying
ambushes and which, in turn, are suspect and must be guarded against,
with what skill to wield the shield, with what whirl the spear,
what prizes may capture a king, what charges may do harm:
such a man will resist all ambushes with steadfast gravity
and guard against wiles with such good sense
that the enemy, broken in combat, cannot achieve by fraud
what he cannot by valor. In such strength did Martin
flourish as a warrior, when the trumpets of Christ
were utterly overthrowing the crimes of a corrupted world.
He knew how to recognize the sign of his King
and to trample these pomps underfoot in the name of the Crucified.
You now counterfeit Christ in a purple robe,
and with gold and gems and the foreign thread of the Chinese
you adorn this guise, wretch, alas, and you cannot deceive.
So, losing so often the frustrated efforts
of your scheming, you melt away again into thin air
and confess your flight by a foul stench.
But you, steadfast in unshaken virtue, triumph,
saint of God, to whom you cleave in unfailing virtue.
Invincible against all sins, you made your character firm:
gentle, patient, just, devout, upright, fair,
mild, confident, humble, kind without gall,
learned, courteous, approachable, easily appeased, keen,
a holy bishop, a good teacher, a beloved host,
wonderful for your signs, and likewise to be imitated for your conduct,
humble in heart, excelling in mind, venerable for both,
you win praise by fleeing it and earn it by shunning it,
drawing out day after day in late-ending fasts
and, always most sparing, with scarcely a little food
refreshing your weary stomach without the weight of meat.
Thus the pleasure of food was driven out, thus that of sleep cast aside,
lest this earthly burden weigh down your wakeful mind,
so that the body might grow used to the light rule of the soul,
as you kept vigil in zeal for prayer and zeal for reading.
Your time clung unbroken to these concerns,
and this alone pleased you as rest: to exchange one labor
for another in turn, in ceaseless, endless prayer.
Let us all marvel, rejoicing, that nature itself
yielded to so great a man. Though the lowest
cleric, forgetful of his great dignity, had wronged him,
he did not swell with gall at the wrong, nor ever, by a judge's
right over those beneath him, burn with desire for vengeance.
Rage did not stir him to hatred, nor joy to laughter,
nor grief to sadness. Holy, with a gravity that commanded reverence,
an angelic countenance shone in his venerable body,
able to display the face of his holy heart
and bring forth the light shut up in his sacred breast.
God was always on his lips, compassion always. Peace
he kept in counsel and in desire. For often envy
would arm jaws tainted with the livid stain of poison
with insults, and kindle even priests with dreadful
gall, so that they preferred to carp at the holy man with their tongues
rather than match him in deeds. Yet even so
anger never drove his holy spirit even to wish to repay them.
Rather, in merciful compassion, his face wet,
he shed brotherly tears for so great a sin,
entreating the Lord Christ with a river of tears
to spare them and grant pardon for their deceitful words.
So, with heart ever steadfast against every wound,
rage did not stir him to hatred, but the cause stirred him to grief:
like the martyr who followed in the Lord's footsteps,
who, receiving the savage onslaught of a cloud of stones,
as he breathed out his fading life from his blessed breast,
begged that their crimes be forgiven the frenzied mob,
grieving more for the people's sins than for the wounds of his flesh.
BOOK FOUR
My translation, once begun, had finished the volume it took up,
running through the pure copies of the holy book,
when suddenly the glory of a hidden history
was offered to us, spurring on the efforts of our vow:
not that it might shine more brightly from my wretched lips,
what the page of so clear a heart had set down,
since the force of the words, flashing with living power,
would lose its native vigor once softened by metre.
But since not all seek to search out from within
the inner depths of the clear spring, and a great many
often drink from open streams close by, passing up its coolness,
we too, who can produce nothing worthy of the learned,
will hold out muddy cups, close at hand, to the sluggish.
Often, too, the piping blown from a rolled strip of bark
tries to match the voices of blaring trumpets,
and he who is used to resting beneath the lofty pine
sometimes makes his way into the thickets of the lowly willow.
You too, who would rather enter pleasant groves,
if perhaps the road to the far-off wood wearies you,
hurry and break into the thicket offered close at hand.
The saint was making his way to the threshold of the blessed church
to offer the customary mysteries to the eternal Christ.
But look: a poor man, trembling with icy cold,
his head shaking, his wretched teeth chattering,
and his hands raised and pressed to his pale cheeks,
was trying to catch a little warmth with his breath.
An icicle formed and hardened his constant tears.
His voice too, sounding pitifully in broken words,
cut short by tearful sounds and speaking in groans,
made plain his whole complaint, his plight crying out for him.
These things might well have softened even a hard severity;
far less could Martin's compassion, already well known,
ignore the distress of this wretched, lamenting man.
At once he commands the deacon standing by, whom, after the custom of earlier
bishops, the prelate had chosen as keeper of the holy treasury,
to buy a garment at his lord's expense and with his money
and quickly fit it on the freezing body.
So what he wished done he left as though it were done,
and then went into the dwelling of a secluded cell,
which, when the saint was about to go out to the sacred mysteries,
was accustomed here too to keep him apart from the nearby crowds,
receiving a monk and soon to send out a minister.
But where will the wretched not force their way, whom distress compels
to lay bare the common shame of a worn and hardened brow?
Where not even priests had access, need broke through,
pleading its plaintive case because the gift had been delayed.
Then indeed pity took hold of his whole mind,
and he did not choose to risk entrusting the order again.
He covered his head with his cloak. Then, with no witness present,
he gradually drew his bent arms in to his body
and, bending forward, shook off the gathered tunic.
Yet his body did not show bare when the poor man was clothed;
so quickly did the outer cloak cover the one who had stripped himself,
that, outrunning the wish of the hurrying poor man, it left
unaware of the deed the very man he had gladdened
with the gift—hidden from the witness, plain to the needy.
Tell me, you who, trampling the joys of a despised world,
have chosen to seek life by casting away your wealth:
who, stripped himself, has covered the naked with his own clothing?
Who, grieving that another bore it, did not shrink from bearing it himself?
Who, willing to be wretched, restored a wretched man by his pity?
You have surpassed, Martin, the examples of the men of old,
and yourself. You were wondrous then, when you covered the poor man
and a portion of the divided cloak still remained to you.
Yield to yourself! By this gift you have doubled your former palm.
Meanwhile, as was the custom, the deacon reminds him that it is the hour
for the solemn rites to be performed in the assembly of the people.
He replies: 'The teaching of the holy prophet must be fulfilled.
Let mercy go before the Mass. This is the more pleasing
sacrifice. Do as you were bidden: first cover the naked man.'
Going out a little way, the deacon looked for the poor man, then came back
and reported that he was gone and could not be found for the gift.
'Come, bring out the gift,' said the saint; 'a needy man will not be lacking.'
Then a garment bought for barely an eighth of a solidus,
woven of knotty threads of bristly wool,
the deacon, annoyed, flings down at the saint's feet.
When the deacon had withdrawn a little, he quickly, rejoicing,
wraps his precious limbs in so cheap a covering.
So the hero goes to the altar, far better adorned
in this garb, like the soldier who, wet with sweat and dust,
runs to meet his king returning after the wars,
the more glorious in honors the more unsightly in limb and face.
For the deed outranks the outward show of virtue, as the strength
of a deep root outlasts the seasons of the leaves.
And no doubtful sign soon proved this offering acceptable.
For while he heaps up the holy gifts with solemn prayer
and accompanies the immortal offerings with sacred words,
a ruddy flame shone out from the crown of his bright head,
pouring splendor on his head yet harmless to his hair,
stretching and rising upward in a clear trail,
breaking through the clear air with a fiery furrow.
Onward, then, O glory, driven by the unceasing round of his honors,
so spurred on by the easy course of his miracles
that, running toward joys with reins wholly slackened,
you take up new things before you leave the finished ones.
There was a certain rich man, Evanthius, who, though bound
by the clinging chains of this world's cares,
was yet of unblemished faith and kindly heart,
keeping his mind pure of earthly sin.
His marrow wholly eaten away by a violent fever,
his trembling insides shaken by rapid breaths,
bursting out in sighs with a sobbing beat,
a suppliant, with the confused murmur of a parched tongue,
the plectrum of his voice hampered by the glue of a dried palate,
often struggling with broken speech
to make his wish known, he asks that the pitiful petitions
of suppliants may obtain for him the saint's speedy coming;
and that if anyone is driven by the burden of pain
or by love of piety, seeking the remedies of health,
let him go to Martin alone: for restoring the span of life,
the sight of Martin surpasses all medicines.
Nor does delay hold back the righteous wish even a little.
He believed that, by God's gift, for the signs he longed for
this faith was enough. And soon the event itself proved it.
Scarcely had even part of the journey's middle stretch been covered
(a great part of the way remained) when grace came ahead of
the traveller. It sent ahead the gifts of the hoped-for health,
a power swifter than his slow limbs going before him.
The healthy man runs to meet the physician. Both rejoice
that, with the body healed, health has been poured into their hearts,
since the healing of the flesh grows from the merits of faith.
So, when the cause of all delay had been removed,
though he wished to return at once, he was overcome by many prayers
and granted the space of a single day, as they had begged.
But what had been brief in time was ample in miracles:
no narrow working makes up for the narrow time.
For a boy, whom an evil serpent had happened to strike
with a deadly blow, infected with the gall of its venom—
when the poison was already swelling his livid limbs,
and the serpent's raging evil, drunk deep into his very vitals,
as though death had already done its work,
was loosening his drooping eyes in hellish sleep—
this boy his master himself, bending his kind back to a just labor,
carried to the holy feet of his true patron,
not doubting, from merits proven by so many signs,
that the one who was present could drive out the poison by touch,
who on his mere coming had put diseases to flight by dread alone.
At once the wound, touched by the medicine of his right hand,
cleansed the chilled limbs of the foul poison;
and wherever the holy hand passed over the body,
death fled and life returned. Soon the plague, gathered together,
withdrew into one place. Then into the wound alone
he packed the poison, ordered to burst out at once,
and the boy, steadying his steps with fearless effort,
ran with undaunted strides while his master rejoiced.
With this reward you go home rich, these gifts you receive,
counting the happy gifts of the health added to you.
What moment was empty of miracles, even on the highway itself?
What road did not reach heaven, though it was a guest upon the earth?
The shepherd was visiting the folds of the flock entrusted to him,
in which the holy Church enclosed the country people,
lest perhaps the tricks of thieves or the fury of wolves
should carry off the unwary sheep while their keeper was away.
Meanwhile, having perhaps left his companions a little behind,
he was going on ahead along the road where the public highway
stretches its raised bank across the level plains,
so that the way, made firm and raised with paving stones,
might shed the pouring rains into the hollows below,
and the heavy wheel-track might not sink into the hard road,
nor the muddy depths swallow up sunken wagons,
but the turning wheels might barely graze the crown of the road,
marking their track with no furrow at all,
but betraying themselves from afar by the ringing of the striking iron.
Along this road Martin was going, a little way ahead,
when suddenly he saw coming toward him a carriage
hurrying in a great whirl, which happened to be carrying men
puffed up with the terror of their military rank. No discipline could curb their fury,
no reason could calm their frenzied minds.
Ambition, drunkenness, shouting, rage, anger, uproar
stirred their unruly hearts with all manner of monstrous passions,
and among the exhausted mules and the terrified drivers
rang the blows of the beaters and the words of the shouters.
There was no rule of stopping in them, nor did any care for danger
slow their swift course over level ground and steep.
These were the men whom the saint, so different in dress and face,
met head on. The beasts feared the awe-inspiring
face of the man before them. Trembling,
the mules, of sounder heart than their masters, swerved from the middle of the road,
their trembling bodies tangled in the twisted harness:
just as once, so Scripture tells, when he was forbidden to curse the holy people,
the ass defied her profane master,
crushing his foot as she pressed her body sideways.
Then, their hearts flooded with a mad poison,
they leap down. Their wish has its hope, their fury its pretext:
they dared even to stretch out sacrilegious hands against the saint
and, vying with one another, to batter the holy body with blows—
him innocent, alone, gentle, calm, patient.
Angry, unsteady, many, swollen with pride, raging,
they shove him, who met their blows without so much as a word;
they hold him, they beat him down. His face is drenched
with blood; his breath bursts from his bruised chest;
his throat is crushed and his gullet turns black and livid;
and his failing eyes, by the light of Christ alone,
make up for the darkness around them. In the gloom of night
his sight fails, but hope shines in his heart.
When his companions saw their master in this state,
the band grew pale and faint at the sight of their patron,
stretching out humble hands to support him
and pressing tender kisses on his bloodied limbs.
Then they hasten to leave the sad place of the dreadful beating.
A donkey stooped beneath and took up the revered burden,
ready to carry its accustomed load. But, his body bent,
the half-dead burden sways, his limbs slumped forward,
and threatens at any moment to slip and fall.
Meanwhile, their hearts sated and their fury spent,
the men went back to the carriage. Then, more swiftly than before,
they force the beasts to burst away at a headlong gallop,
so that whatever delay there had been in the deadly assault
they might at once make up with a whirlwind of speed.
But in vain they set about this effort. The beasts stand fixed
and rebel against the cruel command. Bound
by the Master's will, the mules stood stiff as statues.
Then indeed their anger burns worse, in mad uproar.
Shouts avail nothing, whips nothing. The bruised flanks
resound. They strip the nearby woods for things to beat with.
Stones, stakes, clubs, goads—whatever weapon anger makes
of what each man finds as he searches, he spends on blows.
Yet all this cannot loosen the stiffened sinews
or stir the fixed limbs. You would think them
cold bronze, or figures carved from stone and stiffened there.
At last, when their fury was wholly spent and broken,
their senseless madness let in a sound mind,
so that they knew the mules, held fast amid so many blows,
were numbed by the judgment of God, and that the cause of their delay
had befallen the wretches not without the will of heaven.
Then at last, astonished at the portent, their fury laid aside,
mindful of their sin, they ask who it was who, with his venerable
body, had received the sacrilegious blows of their beating.
And see: on hearing Martin's name, they throw themselves forward
and run to him, their torn hair fouled with dust,
and, wetting their streaming cheeks with a fountain of tears,
humbly wrap their arms around his blessed feet,
begging pardon and confessing their guilt alike.
Nor was the pitiful pleading of the suppliants
long put off: his mercy cut short their long weeping,
and the gift of pardon came before the petitioners' prayers.
At once their freedom to leave was restored: with a word
he swiftly loosened the reins of the delay he had commanded.
Tell me, what can the swift carriage of your king
achieve when God holds it back? Compare brows flashing
with the rays of gems and garments shaggy with bristles,
the titles won by miracles and the pomp of those who command.
Then at least, taught by the weight of the saint's merits,
you will do better to rank his authority above your king.
Go on, then, in unbroken course, and recount the lineage of his miracles
as you compose this history, my Muse, O priest,
and my inspiration. Touch the plectrum of my heart or of my mouth
with your help. Let madmen who speak frenzied things
snatch the Muses to their raving breasts:
let Martin drive us. Such a change of mind
pleases me; for such a fountain my inmost being thirsts.
Let frenzied hearts demand the Castalian waters:
other cups befit men reborn in the Jordan.
Once more the saint was making his venerable way on foot,
where the walls of Chartres lie amid open plains.
So while he passes along the byways of the fertile countryside,
a rightful wonder filled the neighboring village.
Countless people gather from every side; every sex and age
is there. The man's great glory stripped the fields
empty of their farmers. The care of homes now counts for less.
To have seen Martin is enough. At this name even
the pagans themselves rightly stood amazed, as at a title of praise,
and though they had not yet received the power of faith,
they streamed in haste toward the fame of so great a master.
A dense throng of country people crowded close;
a rightful wonder had covered the open fields.
What fruit of salvation from the sowing of so great a crop
you would have rejoiced and longed to store in the barns entrusted to you,
as you looked on stalks still empty of the weight of grain!
Suddenly a mother appears, clasping the lifeless body
of her son, pressing his empty, gaping mouth to her bosom
and thrusting her plaintive breast between his icy lips,
uttering trembling words between her sighs
and wetting her pale cheeks with a river of tears.
His mind, full of God, sensed that the gifts of a favoring God
were near. Grace quickened his pure mind,
so that he trusted that so great a people might be called to the rewards of heaven,
at least once they had seen the Lord's power.
So when the mother, a suppliant, laid the pitiful corpse
of her dead son in his blessed arms,
the limbs he touched began to stir, the eyes unsealed and opened
and little by little grew used to the light poured into them,
and the tongue, striking the plectrum of the moist palate,
shaped into words the voice pressed out from the throat;
and joyfully hanging his arms about Martin's neck,
the boy, ignoring his mother, begged for Martin's embrace.
Open wide your ample bosom, enriched by the peoples you receive,
and joyfully embrace the people added to you,
Bride of God, gathering the whole world to your heart.
But you, idols, long rotting in wretched tombs,
mourn at last the triumphs in which we rejoice.
What hearts did not yield to you, holy one, when you taught?
What fierceness was not made gentle? For always, even in
kings themselves, the hardness set against your wishes
was softened beforehand by the mercy of Christ the Lord.
But fiercer than the rest, and terrible for the vice of pride and anger,
was Valentinian, who then held the throne.
When Martin often approached that ruler as a suppliant,
pleading a difficult cause before a harsh prince,
the king, offended by the petitioner's constant entreaty,
to keep him from often beating on his closed ears with complaints,
orders the saint barred from the doors. Turned away,
he leaves the turbulent halls of the hostile king,
preferring to knock at the threshold of the eternal Christ
and to enter that court which grants to kings themselves
their authority, enclosing their times within fixed bounds,
and binds even stubborn mouths with strong reins.
So his whole mind returns to its accustomed severity,
afflicting the thin flesh on his wearied body,
chafing his wasted skin with a covering of bristles,
spending the day in fasting and the darkness in vigil,
and joining both times together with unceasing weeping.
And if ever his eyes gave way to brief sleep,
the bare ground beneath was enough for his slight slumber,
until Christ, pitying the sorrow of his holy disciple,
sent comfort to his afflicted friend,
brought in a holy message. For, gliding down from on high,
an angel speaks these words of the Lord's command:
'Go on, and enter the barred palace without fear.
Nothing is shut when God has mercy. He for whom the palace of heaven
lay open when he prayed will find these earthly bars open too.'
At once, with so great a guarantor of divine favor,
his faith was sure. Fearless, he makes for the tyrant's threshold
to enter it. The guard of the proud king gave way,
and the weapons posted as sentries of dire threats.
When the king suddenly saw him from his lofty throne,
he was stunned, thunderstruck at the sight, and glared grimly
and threateningly from the royal seat at his trembling servants.
Meanwhile, to find some comfort in slighting the saint,
he deigned no honor to him as he stood close by,
but kept his seat, his limbs unmoving.
But see: in a swift whirl of crackling flame,
a fierce avenging fire, sent by the gift of God,
engulfed the king's throne and part of the man sitting on it.
Then at last, escaping the blaze with a quick leap,
he planted his feet, trembling, his limbs shaken,
glad to pay the holy man the honor wrung from him,
and with kindly feeling to remove the cause of his petition,
submitting his harsh heart to the saint's precepts
and bending his ways, now docile, to his commanding words.
Then too he pressed on him generous gifts, of royal provision.
But the mind rich in God would take nothing
from the world's wealth, leaving earthly
rewards behind and storing up the gifts of the eternal Christ.
Now, since my poor poems in common words
have broken into lofty palaces with humble verse,
we will speak on, in continuing discourse, as Christ grants,
of the heights of kings made subject to the merits of saints.
After, as the page of the book I have gone through recorded,
Maximus had cleared himself of the guilt of the throne he had seized,
he wisely strove with constant services to keep the favor
he had begun to win. For he delighted to summon the saint,
longing to drink from the stream of the divine word
a well-watered faith, and from the fountain of that blessed
mouth to draw the nectar-sweet liquid of teaching,
to learn the honors of the saints and the deeds of the holy,
what battles they sweated through in their struggle, or what
rewards they won as victors, what glory awaits the just
and what punishment the guilty, how the Father's mercy
cherishes, and how heavily the King's sentence strikes.
To him who asked such things the saint gladly
laid each one open and, casting out the darkness, called back the light.
But the queen, no less than her great husband,
diligently outdid even the devoted king in her services.
Hanging always on the holy mouth of the speaker,
and sprinkling his feet, close by, with abundant weeping,
she equaled the merit of her who once with blessed hair
dried the Lord's feet, having first washed them with tears.
But she thinks this little; girded with a special devotion,
she prepares to serve him apart, so that, with the servants sent away,
the happy queen alone might lay the table.
Nor, pressing him often with her husband at her side,
did she cease her prayers until, with constant
tears and unceasing entreaty, she compelled the saint to yield.
She sets the table, places the chair, and of her own accord brings
linen to dry his hands and water to wash them,
and the dishes she had cooked, rejoicing in the service,
she herself hurries to bring in shining baskets.
And whatever time she, never wearied, had free from serving,
she filled with the steady labor of standing in attendance,
and as the reward for so great a work, a venerable gift,
she gathered the scraps of crumbs, so that this food of faith,
made precious by his touch, might satisfy her holy hunger.
O happy woman, who in your virtue set these treasures
above royal riches, choosing rather to serve the blessed man
than to stand above the whole world,
and turning the honor of a reigning queen into the name of a handmaid!
Neither brows radiant with starry gems changed your heart,
nor silks stiff with ruddy threads,
nor gold made more precious by purple woven into it.
By your merit, O queen, you equaled in so great a faith
her who, exalted by the honor of a throne like yours,
came from the ends of the earth to know Solomon,
and travelled far to seek what she already held within herself.
You bring forth the riches of the heart in love of the wise word,
taking in by hearing what you keep with a teachable mind.
Thus you trampled the obstacles of the world beneath you,
a woman made equal to the honors of the men of old.
For often kings unconquered in many a battle
have been fatally conquered by pride alone, refusing the yoke.
Rightly, then, you received the saint's special gift,
that, his severity a little softened and laid aside,
the gentle secrets of his heavenly heart should lie open to you.
How many waves did that holy brow, relaxed into a little calm,
mercifully bid to settle!
How many storms did a gentler breeze calm,
and a clear sky gleaming briefly among the clouds!
How many sorrowful accused this table set free, what bonds
a little freedom, once allowed, loosed, and how many chains
one brief hour shook off as it relaxed its proper rigor!
For time, person and place attend on wise
counsels and steer the mind by sudden reckoning.
Do not hold up to me the name of the female sex,
envious one: not limbs, but hearts will win merit.
Nor is a human being's nature lesser when grace is equal,
nor do nation, sex or age differ in the merit of faith—
man or woman, slave or free, stranger or heir.
It is the believer's merit that counts, not the glory of the flesh.
Finally, what I have learned this sex has earned by faithful zeal,
wishing to touch on it with a few brief signs,
I will relate in whatever words Christ grants.
While the saint, going onward, pursued his venerable journey,
as day turned toward night he made for the nearby
houses and, welcomed under the roofs of a rejoicing village,
he hurried to seek the inner rooms of the holy church.
And here, as always, a guest of the blessed threshold,
he let his weary body rest a little,
loosening his drooping eyes in a short sleep,
so that, renewed by at least a brief and modest slumber,
his very thin limbs might be equal to unceasing labor
and, as its supports, carry his watchful mind.
But when the light, shining out of night, had driven through the darkness,
having quickly and solemnly performed all his duties,
he hastens on his way again. Then indeed a faithful
band of girls, whom holy virginity had consecrated to the Lord,
untouched in flesh and chaste in heart,
lest the frail corruption of the flesh should weigh down to earth
a mind hastening toward the heights of heaven,
burst rejoicing into the inner room of the holy cell,
blessed by its holy guest, and draws in the fresh breaths
and inhales deeply the air still filled with his presence.
Then with humble reverence they venerate the teacher's seat,
and quickly, with the service of their lips, mark each spot with kisses:
where his feet had touched as he stood, where his limbs as he lay,
what had been blessed by his holy food, what pressed by his seat,
or what had lain beneath his limbs as he lay prostrate in prayer.
But when, catching sight of the straw of the blessed bed,
they felt the hay still warm from his holy body,
a violent modesty fights over the prize they have found,
as each seizes a share for herself, and with their bosoms stuffed full,
the packed stalks prick their smooth breasts
and hold their thin garments away from their pricked bosoms.
What can true faith not do? It happened that one of that company
of virgins, no less chaste in heart than in body—
when a demon, holding a certain wretched man by violent claim,
drove him to burst into the frenzies it commanded,
shaking all sound sense out of its captive's breast—
trusting in God's help and the merit of her patron,
wisely lavish with a little of the prize she had seized,
bound about the wretch's throat and hung on the madman's neck
the hay that had been pressed by the blessed body.
At once, terrified by its touch, the enemy
fled the dry stalks as one flees a savage fire,
no match for straw that Martin's body had touched.
And yet, crushed so often and so often put to flight,
you dare, madman, to come against him in changing shapes,
to tempt the man you have already tested, to bring before his face
your fearful eyes, and, disguising your appearance, to display your rage.
For, sitting on a beast's back, and in its frenzy
shaking the butting animal and plunging itself into its entrails,
it had driven out the beast's own nature with deadly rage.
So it was when you weighed down the back of the captive heifer,
so that she bore the monster set upon her not in body alone,
acting out the frenzy poured through her possessed limbs
and suiting her service to the movements of her raving rider,
scattering a bloody dew as she tossed her head,
while red drops ran down her smooth temples
and fiery horns went before her angry brow;
her quick panting could scarcely breathe out one breath after another,
she stirred up a cloud of dust with bent hock,
and her trembling hoof flung the fine sand upward.
Yet after raging here and there among the fleeing crowds,
she grew gentle at the sight of the saint, and when her rider had been put to flight
she stood still; her burden cast off and her mind restored,
the young cow gladly rejoined the herd of her companions.
Now at least stop plunging yourself into the flocks of Christ,
since the saint has not left you any rights even over beasts.
We yield: the glory of his mighty works surpasses the trembling words
of the speaker, a glory displayed in famous deeds
more than it can be uttered in the sounds of the tongue. Let poets
bring dark things to light by their speech; we are overcome by the light of his praise
and, overwhelmed by such splendor, we lie hidden.
And would that the glory of so illustrious a patron,
once we have touched it, might make our night grow a little thinner,
so that we do not cover the light of history with a darkened heart
and the speaker's sins do not lessen the title of his praise.
What heart was not peaceable toward the saint, what rebellious anger,
what savagery was not made gentle? The Molossian hounds felt
his command, when wanton young men out hunting
shook the open plains of the wide fields as they raced across them,
taking slopes and heights alike with a swift leap.
The hurrying horn-hoofed steeds dripped with sweat
and breathed out thin breaths from wide nostrils.
Their galloping hooves rang with a terrifying beat,
leaving a cloud of dust behind their swift tracks.
Yet even so swift a course of winged horses was not enough.
The riders leaned so far forward that their chests were level with the horses' lowered heads,
so that the steeds' slowness held back the wishes of those who sat on them,
and the eagerness of the riders outran the course of their mounts.
The eager Molossians strove to equal the winds
and, in their zeal to win, to satisfy the frenzy of the onlookers,
and from their open throats their tongues hung far out
and shook in their trembling jaws with each gasping breath.
All this great labor, all this expense: to what end, alas, does it come?
What fruit or what profit is there in catching fleeing
little beasts and delighting in the flight of frightened hares?
In your wisdom, Martin, you scorned such frenzy,
pitying the sad plight of the innocent creature, and you made the gaping
jaws of the dogs and their hurrying steps grow numb.
Now, if he happened to relax his unbroken strictness,
with what salt of words he would dispel his companions' cares
and refresh their attentive ears a little,
shrewd yet grave, witty yet devout,
sprinkling the virtue of his heart with the flower of charm!
Seeing a swineherd dressed in a garment of skins,
he said, 'Look, a second Adam! Just such a covering veiled
our naked parent, wrapped around his shivering limbs
and offering a little comfort to his new shame,
when, after the deadly venom of hellish poison,
his deceived body felt the slippery hissing.
But may new grace clothe us again, who have wholly put off
and wholly buried the old sin.'
Likewise, seeing a sheep stripped of its wool, its fleece shorn,
he looked at it with a smile. Then at once,
drawing lessons for teaching from what had happened,
he said, 'See, this lowly sheep has fulfilled the commandment.
Of its two garments it has given one to the one who asked,
unwilling to keep the first while another grows in its place.
How shameful it is for us to fall behind a dumb beast,
if in its lavishness it outdoes us with more generous giving!'
In another place the ridges of the meadows lay open,
each part in a different condition. One part had suffered greedy
swine that rooted it up, and its ridges, black with upturned clods,
had lost their green color.
Another part, its turf gnawed and cropped bare, the herds
had stripped with grim hunger; the mouths of oxen, grazing with heads bowed,
had carried off the mantle of the glad earth,
as the dewy grass is cropped with wide bites,
drawn to the jaws by the roughness of the curling tongue,
which goes ahead and gathers the tender grass with its licking,
so that the greedy teeth may cut the gathered fodder.
No less had the hoof worn it down, pressing with its horny edge
and crushing the green shoots with its frequent tread.
Another part of the field, green with unharmed turf,
nature adorned, dressing it with varied beauty.
The green grasses rippled in the gentle breeze,
and a light wind stirred the blades it pressed.
Over this, countless flowers across the level plain
painted the fields, set with jewels here and there.
Some were tinged with purple and dyed a rosy hue,
while others shone, conspicuous in snowy white,
and among them, marking the grass with saffron patches,
glowed the golden grace of yellow flowers.
Shining drops bent down the jewel-like buds,
and amber beads of moist dew bowed the grasses.
A sweet scent, vying to equal the pleasing color
and blending harmonious delights with forms as lovely,
fed the eyes with beauty and the nostrils with fragrance.
Scattered leafy boughs gave most welcome shade,
and dark-blue arms nodded with intertwined branches.
Birds hidden in the leaves vied in singing of spring,
tuning their musical whistles with sweet-sounding tongues.
A clear brook fed the grass nearby
and, brushing the blades, nourished them with its gliding moisture.
Beneath, pebbles that the gaze could see right through to
rippled the glassy waters with their gentle obstruction,
nor could the depths take their submerged beauty from the eyes:
their form lay open to sight, though covered by the stream.
Why do I try to describe these forms in crude speech?
Words cannot express these things, which, by the gift of Christ,
the grace of nature has better shaped and painted.
Seeing, then, this scene marked out in such unlike forms,
Martin said, 'Compare for a moment
each part of the meadow, the grazed, the dug-up, and the unharmed,
with the sin of harlots, with wives joined in lawful
marriage, and with virgins, who vow to Christ
holy bodies adorned with the jewels of rosy modesty.
As in that dug-up field no beauty remains,
so the image of Christ does not shine when smeared with vices.
As here the root remains safe, though the grass is cut,
so married women keep their faith secure, though without the flower of virginity.
As color and brightness smile in the flowering field,
so the glory of pure flesh will shine brightly.'
As he was giving such lessons of clear-sighted strength
and of a heart always intent on divine rewards,
a certain monk came to him, who had won this name by abandoning
military service, and who, after the trumpets and bugles of war,
had chosen to give himself to the standards of the true King,
following to better purpose the great banners of the holy cross.
Indeed, he had drawn his wife into a fellowship of life
and had instructed her to be a companion of the holy
virgins, giving up the rights of the marriage bed and of the flesh.
But when wanton desire revived and began once more
to goad his mind and to plant deep in his marrow
the mortal joys of the world he had scorned,
longing to loosen the strictness he had barely tasted,
running back again to the embraces and desires of the married,
and to take up again, after the title of monk, the name of husband,
he even set about assailing his teacher
with frequent clamor, mixing such complaints with his pleas:
'If Christ grants me the comforts of marriage,
having deigned to join the two sexes in wedlock,
who will snatch God's gifts from me? Who will dare, with a new law,
to overturn the ancient law of the Lord?'
As he broke out in such grumbling with headlong mind,
the holy patron's healing approached him gently:
'Come, tell me, if you recall the times of your past life,
whether you ever fought a cruel enemy in pitched battle.
Since you remember that this happened very often,
consider likewise whether, amid the trumpets and bugles of war,
the javelins poised in the fighters' fearsome arms,
the drawn swords, and the silken dragon standards swollen with the wind
imitating the coils or the fury of serpents,
the female sex ever disgraced the ranks of battle.
What place is there for spinning among shields, or for girls among arms?
Did a sprinkling of dust ever suit smooth faces?
But if these things are not fitting for earthly camps,
so that nothing feminine becomes the standards of men,
then for you, who wage war with unceasing sweat,
will not mingling with the sex you spurned be all the more shameful?
In times of idleness let wanton pleasure
find such a laughable troupe; but when manly
battle lines hasten to the field and iron-clad ranks gleam,
let walls protect the throngs of women,
and let them, having no trust in arms, take care to shut themselves behind the gates.
But let the man who hastens to war scorn such comforts.'
With such words he healed the wounds of the unbridled mind,
gave new joys once more to the heart now set at rest,
and sent the fighting man back to his wars in peace.
Now who could worthily recount this:
how great the patience that adorned so teachable a gentleness?
Once, among maidens holy in both heart and flesh,
precious flowers [?] of everlasting chastity,
whom unwed virginity, devoted to Christ, had joined to the Lord
by a bond of the mind, not by a covenant of the flesh,
there was one who had surpassed them all in zeal for virtue,
adding this special distinction to the honors of her chastity:
that, having once withdrawn from the eyes of all men,
she kept the strict rule she had begun with a steadfast heart,
and did not waver with the unsteady mind of a fickle woman,
surpassing by the weight of her virtue her inborn sex
and even the rare examples of men of earlier times.
Just admiration for this resolve moved the saint,
rightly honoring such a maiden, to visit her,
drawn by so great a flower of virtues.
But her faith, already vowed to the Lord, remained so firmly fixed
in her steadfast breast that the bars of her chastity,
closed to men and guarding the honors of her glorious palm,
could not be unlocked even by the merit of so great a patron.
Yet his faith, rejoicing in her resolve, did not blush
to bear a refusal it welcomed; rather, in his kindness,
he counted all that had given him hope as an honor to himself,
heeding the soul's gain more than the joys of the flesh.
What part, what part will you snatch from that holy breast,
Ambition, puffed up by the winds of mad swelling?
Lie now utterly prostrate. Christ can have nothing
in common with vices. Those who swell with praise
long to exalt themselves. But he who wishes to remain hidden
and scorns the heights of the world proves clearly enough
how fully he yields to the Lord alone the honor that he shuns.
But you, who would rather be thought little of so that Christ may be praised,
adding this judgment too to your blessed honors,
by shunning the praise you flee, you deserve it all the more.
BOOK FIVE.
Once already brought forth in praise of so great a patron,
why, my tongue, are you silent, shutting up the rough murmurs of your voice
and your untaught sounds in long silence?
If it makes you blush to speak of such great things, that law for your modesty
should have been laid down earlier. All too late
you try to draw this veil over a brow already all too worn.
But if you are held in the base torpor of sloth,
then, so that the grim image of foul death may depart,
shake off the languid sleep from your weighed-down breast,
so that, wakeful, with death dispelled, you may rise again to Christ.
If you lie low as you deserve, trust in your patron.
Why tremble as one liable to punishment, when you are liable only to a vow?
Come then, commit your spent ember to the Lord,
so that the stiffness of my wit may grow warm as Christ breathes on it,
and Martin's prayer may melt the ice of my heart
and make the dumb voice burst forth at once,
as once he won the miracle of a like deed.
Where the walls of Chartres lie among open plains
and Gaul stretches far and wide in boundless fields,
there a daughter who had been mute for twelve years,
her mouth blocked, unopened to any speech,
the saddest care of her grieving parents,
by living only increased the unending sorrow of the wretched pair,
and with the passing years the wounds of their grief grew.
Alas, how often they grieved that the gifts of mighty God, granted to others,
had been lost for them, when they often saw
little ones, barely crawling, burst out into words
and names come out half-broken from tender lips,
when fond love, running ahead, took note of each uncertain murmur,
recognizing the faltering voice with affection as its interpreter,
catching the sounds as if they were words and seizing on what was yet to be said.
These things, granted to others soon after the cradle,
their envious love had bewailed for twelve years,
as, grieving through two five-year spans and two years more,
it longed for her first word by the time she was of age to marry:
until, clasping Martin's knees and clinging to them,
the father, half-dead, pitiful, his face streaming with tears,
laid out his whole complaint, his groans making it plain,
drawing up sighs from the depths of his breast,
breaking his tearful murmur with frequent sobs,
and drenching his wet breast with the rain from his cheeks.
And already love of his accustomed compassion had stirred
Martin's kindly mind. But the cause of his delay
lay in his integrity, his care for precious modesty,
and the humility that must always be joined to famous deeds,
lest boasting should lose the merit the deed had brought
and presumption of heart corrupt the work of virtue.
So he said: 'I think myself unworthy of the miracle of so great a deed,
and with trembling neck I dread the weight
which in my weakness I cannot bear, lest too great a burden
press me down and I struggle, too feeble, beneath an excessive load.
But no cure whatever is difficult for Christ,
who rightly entrusts these signs to other ministers,
so that the Lord's miracles may reveal the merit of the saints.
See, two men stand here, renowned for integrity, faith,
and virtue, whom such a life has rightly raised
to this office. Will not the Lord's healing grant more readily to them
these things, which, great as they are, exceed
our merit, but are not hard for saints?'
Often repeating such proofs of a modest heart,
and proving his merit by refusing it, he stands out the worthier for this,
that precious modesty adorns his other virtues,
and he escapes envy who fears to put himself forward.
Seeing this, the father presses the saint more urgently,
adding to his prayers those very men whose faith
Martin had said should be chosen, so that he might not even be allowed to put off
what a kindred will, by Christ's inspiration, had piously urged,
along with the grace of an equal and harmonious authority.
So the crowds were sent away, lest perhaps the throng, if admitted,
should drown out the one praying with its confused murmuring,
or boasting display its own powers;
he took as companions only those whom the summit of honor
had made his equals, and who shared an equal care for prayer,
equal zeal, linked faith, united will.
The trembling father too was added, whom his vows,
as he longed the more keenly for Christ's gifts, made faithful.
Then, raised up in lofty spirit but prostrate in body,
setting his holy heart on high but his limbs below,
he lies low in the flesh but is strong in mind. His mind, joined to God,
climbs on high; the pride of the flesh is pressed down.
Thus unlike paths are joined in one harmonious act,
thus the humble hasten where the faithful have gone before.
Without delay the saint perceived the signs of the accustomed favor,
for he rejoiced constantly in Christ as his guest,
often opening the doors of his heart to such gifts.
Then he ordered oil to be brought out for blessing,
steeping the liquid offered him in the nectar of his words,
through which healing came into the transformed fluid.
Once it was poured into the mouth of the grateful girl,
at once the bonds of her knotted tongue were loosed,
and, filling her moistened throat with sudden breath,
a sweet-sounding murmur, the long-awaited voice, came to life.
And first he bade her mark her trembling speech properly
and shape her uncertain sounds into her father's name.
This was her first word, and from the speaker's lips, the first time they spoke,
her father snatched it and, once heard, sank it deep in his heart.
Then he falls prostrate at the saint's feet
and, a suppliant, embraces his knees with outstretched arms.
And he who alone had brought prayers while the girl was silent
now repays thanks to the Lord with more than one voice.
Nor indeed is the wonder of another deed any less,
which the pouring of healing liquid
and the blessing of oil prayed over have brought to my mind.
Whenever healing called for the aid of compassion,
the same grace sanctified this oil for different needs.
For as the faithful, with provident hearts, often do,
they either offer to righteous men a vessel filled with oil
to fulfil their prayers for preserving health, or reverently place it
in holy places: places where either a present working
reveals by its power the patrons who have won their martyr's discharge,
or where the Word came into the blessed cradle,
as manifest faith recalls and the reading of Scripture declares,
or where, cutting short the hours of continuing daylight
and shuddering at the deadly crime of a dreadful people,
night spread across and brought in sudden darkness,
or where the blessed hollow of the cleft rock,
rejoicing at God's touch, free from the law of the tomb,
lay open beneath limbs that were soon to rise again,
or where the happy earth, rejoicing in Christ's return to the stars,
received his last footprints from this world;
and that ground, preserving the gift of so sanctifying a touch,
has scorned whatever adornment a skilful hand devised
and cast it far from its sands,
bursting the fragile lattice as the dust pours through it,
and breaking up the metal enclosures laid over it:
in these places, very often, those whose nearness allows it
set out the peaceful liquid in clean little vessels,
to be transformed by the nectar of dew poured down from above,
through which heavenly grace flows into the holy liquid.
But those whom long stretches of road lying between
keep far removed in a distant region,
believing that the Lord is not shut in by the boundaries of places
and that the help of the Merciful One goes beyond all limits,
with unhesitating faith ask for present gifts
from a present Lord, who, by the power of his favor,
does not wear out the prayers of those coming to him with long journeys,
but touches everywhere those who pray, brought near to him,
nor does he shun the slow, and stands closer to the swift,
and the traveler's effort alone becomes the journey's end.
Those who bear this in their hearts, in whatever region they call on him,
possess the Lord's gift, whether they entrust their prayers
to holy men or lay up whatever is to be hallowed
in consecrated places. What Christ did not visit in his holy body
he covers by his power, though, having returned
to the heights of heaven, he has long reigned there in his body too.
Often turning these things over as faith spurred her on,
a woman who surpassed her frail sex by the strength of her faith,
lofty, and with no womanish heart,
believed, when she sent oil to offer to the saint,
that the compassion brought near through the prayers of so great a minister
would favor her prayers, with Martin praying, no less
than if, carried swiftly in rapid flight,
she were bringing her prayers into the very tomb of the Lord,
embracing the standard of the cross and the wood of salvation.
Full of such faith, she carefully poured into gleaming glass,
with anxious hands, the green oil.
The descending stream changes the snowy color,
and flowing with silent fall into the hollow beneath,
it rises little by little as the shining liquid increases,
and swells richly in silence, without a sound.
Yet, so that the empty neck might stay open for the stopper
and the flask not slop over, overfilled with the stream,
where the neck rises from the round body below
a wide gap of still-empty mouth remained.
Then the servant took the oil and hurried off
to the saint, conveying both the prayers and the words of his petitioner.
Nor is the work of compassion slow. Swift grace commends
righteous zeal, lest by hesitating it put off the faithful
or a short delay make its favor doubtful.
And at once God showed by signs he granted
how great a gift the present blessing would bestow,
lest perhaps faith should falter with a trembling mind.
The men present were amazed (for Christ had willed
that chosen witnesses be present at so great a miracle)
that the liquid had so grown as Martin prayed
that the wave, rising in an upward swell,
filled the empty part with its suspended flood;
thus, constantly hastening to the top yet never leaving the bottom,
it seethed as it overflowed and, settling, stayed full;
it grew from what was poured in, yet would not be emptied by what was taken out:
until the servant, carrying the happy gifts back to his mistress,
went off exultant, and his right hand, rejoicing in such signs,
presented the merit of the blessed man.
Such was the holy blessing of the illustrious prophet
when the widow had lavishly spent her meager store:
it filled her empty vessels with lasting gifts,
so that she who had given proofs of generous faith
grew richer by her spending, secure in what she had asked.
Indeed, though I dread to touch the man's other praises
and wonders, I shall at least be able to tell of these,
in which a like blessing of the same liquid
rightly calls for heralding with many voices.
One faith, frequent healing: they do not differ in kind of act,
but differ in number; alike in signs, different in gifts.
Here is a witness, Severus, wonderful for his learned speech,
who followed Christ with the whole strength of his heart,
distinguished by worldly titles, but more famous for the way
he despised the world through the power of holy faith,
powerful in noble rank, but far more eminently
ennobled by the worship of Christ than by birth and blood.
He, condensing the sacred canon and the writings of far-reaching history,
enclosed it all in two little books,
whatever he had surveyed of what was recorded from the first ages.
He too, recounting Martin's honors and deeds,
a careful investigator of the truth and a faithful reporter,
brought before the public the distinctions of so famous a life,
keeping a just balance with even scales,
so as neither to assert doubtful things nor keep silent about certain ones.
He very often clung devotedly to the saint as his companion,
as a kindred mind, seen in the mirror of the heart,
is wont to join together like shapes of character.
All the more, then, must we believe a witness who is the more proven,
who teaches what he learned face to face, since he tells of things seen.
So among other tokens of affection he asked
to receive a special gift of the holy liquid.
After the blessed man, rejoicing, had granted it to his faithful friend,
an aid of power and a memorial of favor,
he carried it home with reverent faith,
believing that he was bringing with him the health that had been granted,
and set it high up in a lofty window,
where panes stretched across shut in the clear daylight,
facing the blasts of the winds and open to the light.
There he covered the flask with a snowy cloth,
so that the linen spread over it might keep off roving glances
that would meet the eye, though it would not shut out minds.
But a servant, unaware, with a sweep of his hurrying hand,
while hastily snatching the covering with careless effort,
struck the glass vessel and sent it down onto the marble below.
The servant stood stunned and bloodless, his master turned pale,
and the sound rebounds with a rapid beat to the roof,
and the ringing, filling everything at once with its roving murmur,
dashed against the heights and rose from the depths.
The flask, struck, did not feel such crashing blows,
and its covering of glassy shell remained unharmed.
So the liquid within, enclosed in its fragile garment,
had hardened the outer walls of the hollow vessel,
so that you would think the marble had been changed wholly into feathers
and had caught that fall on soft cushions.
Thus your merit, Martin, thus your constant grace
devotedly receives what is sanctified and guards what is blessed.
A certain man, when the savage violence of a fearsome Molossian hound
rushed at him, its jaws gaping from its raging throat,
its wrinkled muzzle drawn back from the covering of its lips,
gnashing its bared teeth with constant snarling,
terrified by so sudden a fright, not with a stick or a blow
but by Martin's name alone shut its rabid mouth.
As soon as the name rang out, the barking stuck, held back,
the bristling hackles fell, and the menacing, grim,
bulging eyes, their flames suffused with blood,
laid aside their threats and closed. Then it began gently to lower its ears
and to sweep the ground with its wagging tail
and to bow its head with neck bent low.
What would not yield, made gentle, to your merits, Martin,
when you overcome such rage by your name alone?
Why should we now wonder that the hearts of savage men
give way and human passions grow gentle before you?
So once men were astounded that the dread power
and authority of cruel Avitianus yielded to you,
to whom ferocity was all too closely bound, and whose only pleasure
was the hook, executioners, torturers, whips, chains,
the death of men, the cries of mourners and the pallor of the accused,
the devouring prison, death for the one who confessed, torments for the one who denied.
This most savage beast, with a heart all too hellish,
breathing countless slaughters from his raging breast,
roaring with pitiless ferocity, had entered the city
which Martin governed as bishop with holy honor.
There, bound by chains linked around their filthy necks,
clung together a pale, unhappy file of grieving prisoners,
rattling their screeching chains against broken limbs
and moving [?] slow steps with bent breasts.
Leading such a spectacle before Martin's eyes, this Phalaris
prepares all manner of slaughter at the nearby tribunal.
His rabid ministers, a frenzied throng, hasten,
vying with one another to seek out instruments for savage punishments.
Some bring out vessels for hellish flames,
in which, with the heat of dread vapor shut inside,
melted pitch would feed the crackling of the fierce fire,
which, overflowing far with its flood of deadly flame,
would roast the body caught in its sulphurous cavern.
Others, with raging hearts, were preparing (a grim task)
beams of timber stretched upward,
so that the flesh, hanging cruelly from limbs swiftly stretched,
might expose its torn limbs to the torturer for torment,
drenching his hellish right hand with the wretch's blood
and spattering the grim gore through wound after wound.
And so that the same punishment might sate a double fury,
the striker shook the joints of the mangled body,
tearing apart the bonds of the limbs as their knots burst.
Still others were bringing torches and coating with much grease
long bands of woven papyrus,
not so that their light might dispel and conquer the darkness,
marking the dark night with fire-streaming light,
but so that a deadly fire might burn the wretches,
thrusting flames brought close against their torn limbs.
Was it fitting that such things be seen in Martin's city,
and that his calm mind be pierced by so great a wound,
even if only the report of it reached his holy ears
or rumor alone shook his tender heart?
So when his mind was struck by these deadly preparations,
and a messenger had spread word of the dread tyrant's savage contrivances,
forerunning signs of the fury close at hand,
just pity ran through his very marrow
and the flame of compassion spread a swift heat.
And though clemency, mindful of human misfortunes,
compelled him to weep for the death of the wretched accused,
there was no lesser cause of present grief:
that the very man who avenged crime was abetting wickedness,
and by punishing guilt would first make himself guilty.
A thicker darkness had wrapped and covered the world.
Welcome rest had spread soothing sleep through all the elements,
all things lay languid in dewy slumber,
and the murmurs of hushed voices were silent, suppressed.
The deep silence of midnight was all too awesome,
and the dark gloom poured over everything had covered
every color, robbing all shapes of their outlines.
But Martin had no thought of taking rest;
rather, holy prayers for the safety of men stood by him,
as love spurred his mind. So he makes for the bloody
judge's hellish threshold with urgent step.
Alone and undaunted he goes through the dark silence of vast
night and the obscure, fearsome solitudes of the roads.
I believe indeed that all the troops of shades gave way,
whom the evil demon stirs up to crimes of the night,
and that the fearsome hounds, savage at other times, fell gently silent,
their barking stuck, blocked in their terrifying mouths.
So when he reached the barred threshold of the dread
judge and the deadly stronghold of savage fury,
lying prostrate in the roadway before the house, he is kept out
by the closed doors, but with his weeping knocks at the stars.
The savage beast was breathing out heavy sleep from his swollen breast,
and, sprawled in the image of death,
had flung his torpid limbs full length upon his bed,
when suddenly an angelic terror shook him to his depths,
and a voice burst into the astonished ears of the stupefied man:
'Has wretched sloth weighed you down in heavy sleep,
you beast, belching up cups of corrupted wine,
and has the load of an undigested belly swollen you in your sluggishness,
while the Lord's servant, on the dry back of the bare earth,
covering his holy body with thick dust,
lies—look!—before your doors? Do you set bars against him
for the sake of the night's silence and your shameful sleep?'
He froze at the sudden vision and hastily summoned
his servants, ordering them to go out swiftly to the gate
and bring back word of the truth of the matter.
But as welcome rest often binds and overcomes
the weighed-down senses when the limbs are bound in torpor,
the servants, going only a little way, barely to the outer threshold,
heavy-eyed and stumbling in their steps,
return a deceitful mumble in muddled words:
no one had been found at the doors after careful search.
Again the pleasure of sleep, close at hand, not far removed,
at once closed his drowsy eyes.
Then indeed a new terror shakes his trembling heart,
and the threatening sentence of the angelic voice,
repeating its command, forced him to rise headlong.
Nor did he care to risk entrusting the command to others again.
He himself hurried with swift step to the closed threshold,
and the barred doors open as the master unlocks them.
The venerable bishop shone out with radiant face,
displaying in his holy countenance the crown of virtues.
Grace flourished in him, shining with many signs,
in devotion, faith, affection, compassion, and modesty:
a mind cheerful in hardship, steady and serious in joy,
neither stiff with harshness nor letting its gravity dissolve in laughter,
always shining with a balanced integrity,
so that neither anger made him fierce nor kindness slack.
Such was the venerable figure that met the pale tyrant,
breaking through the clouds of foul night.
And already his mind, conscious of so great a crime, had revealed without words
what the reason was for that holy labor,
nor did it need to be laid bare by pleading. He himself first, confused,
brought forth a fearful voice from his trembling breast:
'Why, holy one, with fear as my torturer, wearying my heart so long,
do you trouble me, shaking sleep from me entirely?
You are kept far off by the doors, yet you break into the inner chambers
by your holy merit. You stand back in body, yet by right
you enter; you shake me with terror while you stay outside in the flesh.
Nor indeed would I deny that this is owed to my deserts,
since with a hard heart I breathed out countless slaughters,
raging in your city. I beg you, then, pardon one who confesses;
use your right. You wish them spared: let them be released.
Free the accused from punishment, and free me from guilt.'
Without delay the chains were loosened and fell away at once,
which only a moment before had bound the necks of the pale accused,
keeping their dying bodies for a dreadful death.
Suddenly hope, restored to the wretches' prayers, leaps for joy.
With joy mingled with fear, so great a thing so suddenly
they tremble to believe, yet would rather believe.
They vie in gratitude to throw themselves at the holy man's knees
and fondly clasp his feet with suppliant arms.
He urges that thanks should rather be given to God,
and admonishes them that Christ is the author of this deliverance,
who spares crimes in this way, provided that true conversion
at least shows sorrow for the wickedness committed;
for punishment awaits the guilty while their guilt endures.
Laboring with such words and with compassion alike,
he freed the prisoners from punishment and released them from their sins.
Now what tongue could worthily speak of this gift,
which my mind, too narrow for the honors of so famous a patron,
fears even to touch with its astonished sense:
that the saint's merit so terrified all the troops
of the devil, and the signs of their great fear were so plainly shown,
that whenever he went out from the threshold of his own cell
and turned his steps toward the city, lying some way off,
to visit the people committed to his holy governance
or wishing to offer the mysteries of the sacred rite,
grace, going swiftly before him in rapid flight,
so tormented the trembling specters in the bodies they held captive
that, when he had scarcely left the inner rooms of his holy dwelling,
they perceived through torments that ran far ahead of him
that he would soon be there, and with the shrieking murmur of their voices
the punishment of the guilty proclaimed the coming of the judge.
And when he had set his first steps in the doorway,
one could see bodies, their limbs swiftly snatched on high,
bound by airy bonds and lifted up,
and the swaying weight of heavy flesh, through empty space,
leave the nearby earth in a rapid whirl,
hanging in their own punishment, yet free of any bond,
bound by the merits of his prayers, suspended in their own penalties,
crying out their committed faults before a silent judge.
Nor was it a confession given in answer to a questioner's words
that, wrung out by a trembling voice, revealed their crimes.
For, lying on the ground, the saint passed beyond the stars in prayer,
touching the Lord in hope, though prostrate in body,
humble in heart, lofty in merit, crying out without a sound,
a judge hidden from sight, proven by his power,
at whose merit such great miracles were displayed:
the culprit hanging in empty space, its own torturer in the air,
feet stretched upward, yet its clothing, held stiff,
clung to the limbs it covered,
so that it would not, folding over or slipping back,
lay bare the shameful parts of the hanging body.
Thus your merit, Martin, thus the holy power
and the glory of God, to be revealed through the servants of Christ,
going beyond the earth in its honors, reigns in the air as well.
It is certain, too, that at your entreaty the clouds were dried up,
and the dread downfall of hail hung suspended,
the flood of the thickened storm cloud wholly held back,
which, heavy, its waters hardened into stones
by the binding chill of the stiff wind, in whirl upon whirl
used to hurl to earth stones of solid water,
so that crops, shrubs, gardens, orchards, and vines
were crushed by the storm's weapons in ruin upon ruin,
and the earth, pitted, was shaken by mighty blows.
This plague, rampaging far and wide through the fields of the Senones,
and accustomed to carry out the law of its punishment every year,
had stripped the fields bare, battered by constant ruin.
The pale plowman told of his lost harvest,
lamenting the heads of the stalks utterly broken down,
and the vine-dresser, often groaning over his vine, empty of fruit and shoots,
after the year-long hopes of unceasing labor
counted his losses among clusters that had already been swelling.
The sorrowing mother pointed out the broken branches
to her children, used to clambering up to the mellow little apples,
and beside the pale shoots of the parched field
the rocks rang, echoing with the lowing of cattle.
Wasted herds wandered through empty hollows,
bearing witness to their plaintive cause with what groans they could.
Driven, then, by this evil, the whole people, of every age,
longing to win so famous a patron for themselves,
humbly entreat Martin through an envoy as their spokesman
to strive to appease God and to beg pardon
for the wretched, and at last to drive away the grievous plague.
[saying] that enough punishment had been paid, so that the clemency of Christ
might take away the excessive disaster, at least after the scourging.
Nor indeed did the hope they waited for deceive the wretched people.
For as soon as Martin, ever joined to the Lord and clinging to him,
asked for the gifts of his accustomed loving-kindness,
they felt his devout intercession: the storm was driven off
and fell still, and the days shone with a pure, clear sky,
or else the young shoots were moistened by longed-for rains.
Nor was this grace confined to a brief span; for a long time,
commending its gifts all the more gratefully by its extended bounds,
it lasted through four full five-year spans,
nor did they feel the damage of a raging storm until
the Lord, having closed the time of this present life,
took his blessed friend to true rest.
So he spent the time of both lives devoutly:
before, salvation to the earth; now, on high among the stars.
But now the overlong page of a flagging book
weakens the honors and deeds of the illustrious patron.
While I, a small man, speak of great things, and sluggish, of sublime ones,
as a trembling narrator I spoil the splendor of his praise.
But what am I to do? I vowed to run through the history in verse:
what is told fears judgment; what is suppressed fears the charge of guilt.
Better that a reader should perhaps abandon these things in distaste
than that a devout listener should miss what had been wholly left out.
My earlier discourse has already touched before on the pitiless Avitianus;
now the order of the work is called back to him.
He, who surpassed savage tyrants in dreadful ferocity,
thirsting for the grim tortures of wretched defendants,
was a little milder and spared the city of Tours.
Here alone he showed traces of human feeling:
he submitted his mouth, rebellious though it was, to the saint's reins,
curbing his inborn fury at Martin's commands.
And indeed clear proofs of this cure
appeared one day in this way. The venerable Martin
was approaching the dreadful seat of so harsh a judge,
so that his ferocity might grow gentler and soften through such
kind services, bound by the attentions of the holy patron.
He happened to be sitting on a lofty seat,
towering on a conspicuous throne and swelling with excessively proud
ambition, when suddenly the saint, looking at him,
sees the bloody form of a bristling, foul
and raging demon reclining on his neck,
fastened there and lying prone upon him with all its weight.
When the saint touched it from afar with the breath of his blessed mouth
and put it to flight by bringing the terror of his word to bear,
Avitianus, unaware of the companion he bore, believed that he himself
had received a heavy penalty in the form of a curse.
Martin replies: 'Do not suppose that you have been branded
by my judgment, or that this is the sign of some sudden outburst.
It was love, not anger, that raged against the enemy;
in pity for the wretched it grieves. Against him burst forth
this breath of mine from the very depths of my heart,
the one I saw pressing down this lofty bench with horrible weight
and lying prone upon your neck.
Cease now to put up with the partnership of such a robber;
trust rather in devout counsels. Let his cunning, now detected,
be put to flight; let caution, having learned his tricks, drive him off.
Be ashamed now to obey a guilty one, to serve one who has been routed.'
By such words the door of his heart was shut to the expelled
demon, and its power over its seat was snatched away.
From then on the judge was gentler, at last free of a judge over himself,
and the heavy burden was cast off from his freed neck.
Thus in every place he drove the enemies from their seats and put them to flight,
setting free the hearts of men and leaving not even temples to the fugitives.
For whatever shrines vain error had built,
he burned to lay waste far and wide in headlong ruin.
Not far distant from the aforesaid city
there was a village, once the remains of an old fort,
now inhabited by servants of God and ministers of Christ.
Its former inhabitants called it by the ancient name of Amboise.
Here a towering temple of immense workmanship had been built
long ago by the senseless madness of a sacrilegious company.
Rising into a cone, the towered mass stretched up on high,
a marvelous work, with its stones fitted so perfectly
and joined throughout, though in close-packed courses,
that the lofty weight could not totter nor any crack gape,
but a handsome bond held the stones laid together.
All the more did those who lacked reason stand amazed, with astonished minds,
at the craftsman's skill. So shamefully foolish
a religion grew strong, worshipping as divine nothing but
the builder's talent, and making a god's genius out of his name.
This temple, then, the holy Martin had ordered to be overthrown.
He reproaches a faithful priest for orders long neglected.
But he modestly
denies that these commands could have been carried out. He shows that these tasks
were far too hard for weary monks and a few ministers of God,
tasks which crowds gathered from an emptied countryside could scarcely
accomplish, or cohorts sweating at the work.
In these words a just excuse was fully plain.
Yet his hope was not broken. He does not plan to summon
the peoples, nor hasten to lead troops gathered from all the world
to the village of Amboise.
He calls on heavenly help. All his hope is in him
who rules heaven and earth, for whom the air does service as a soldier
and the elements keep an abiding awe.
Once more, then, came the bristly garment, accustomed to pierce with its goads
