the skin of the one lying in it, fleece knit with stubborn
harshness out of stiff threads to wound;
once more wakeful groans, once more fasts
renewed with food put off, joining the labor of night
once more to the sun that soon would follow.
Nor did long delay put off the answer to this prayer. See, when day returned,
a violent tempest roars around the temple,
as the clouds burst into rivers in a whirlwind of winds.
The clouds split apart as the lightning flashes out,
and the mass of gathered waters on the heights
dashes against the building's frame with a hoarse-roaring whirlwind,
and the battle of the clouds gives forth a crushing crash.
The earth trembled and, shaken from its lowest depths,
spat out the tottering foundations of the mass set upon it,
scattering the ruin far from its bonding
and rolling the fragments of the shattered mass down the slopes.
O you beloved of God beyond measure, at your supplication Christ
once dried up rain clouds already sinking low in the high air;
now at your prayers swift storms have returned again,
and clouds black and girded with heavy winds,
commanded to spare the crops while bursting mighty masses,
gentle to the grass and pitiless to hard stones.
Nor will this next merit be any less, nor, from a cause not unlike,
its glory unequal, as it imitates the same triumphs.
The towering supports of a column raised an idol's image
far up on high on stones joined together,
so that the figure, loftier and more exalted on that throne,
might look down on the wretched people with its feigned divinity.
Martin longed to overthrow this mass too,
but all the means for such a wish were lacking to him;
yet his hope always remained swift to turn to the Lord.
So when he flew back to heaven with swift mind
and asked quick help from the King of heaven,
a fiery column, like in form but unlike in light,
came gliding down and shattered the fragile structure into ruin,
its sulphurous flame rolling up crackling embers,
raising a smoking cloud from the burnt dust
and an overflowing vapor once the mass was consumed.
So, Martin, by the glowing sky, so by the whirling wind,
you link twin triumphs, one by cloud and one by fire.
Nor is it a wonder that the Lord fulfilled his promises to so faithful
and holy a servant, he who had once told
his servants, utterly astonished at such great miracles,
that he would give these proofs of true faith:
that those who believed would show greater signs than these.
What wonder is it that the Lord graciously accomplished the same things
through his servants, he who deigned to promise more to his devout ministers
and called their hearts upward to the heights?
For just as the page of the heavenly book relates,
bearing witness to a woman's faith, that after a long flow
of blood and a grievous wasting that had consumed her body
swift health returned at the touch of a garment,
so the glory of the same deed was given to Martin,
but it was God who healed, who now too, on high in the citadel
of his starry throne, is shown to be touched through the members
that cling to the eternal Head in holy union.
What monster was not gentle to the devout man, what monster not subject
to the faithful man? Snakes often obeyed when commanded,
and no native ferocity remained in their conquered venom.
A dreadful serpent was swimming across by the nearby shallows
and furrowing the glassy waters. Its head stood out of the waves
together with its neck. With its breast it cleft the surface of the river
in haste. The rest of its length, through the blue water,
bent its slippery curves in shifting motion,
twisting the curved coils of its nimble tail
and flickering its quivering tongue, intent on wounding.
When Martin saw it, barely midway across the water,
hurrying on and just about to reach the nearby shore,
with these words he forced it to turn back at once,
bound by the power of God and the name of Christ:
'I command you by no means to press on any further
to the forbidden bank.' The evil beast stopped in mid-stream,
and a rigid numbness bound its broken limbs,
and little by little its body stuck fast, its swimming held captive,
until, its course through the blocked flood shut off,
its limp neck floated, surrendered to the deep,
and the sluggish channel carried the half-dead snake back.
And oh, that with like power my own venom,
which the slipperiness of a life badly run has tainted,
forever plunging my sins in the rushing flood of this world,
might be turned back by the faithful compassion of the holy patron,
and that he might compel it to remember again the salvation it forgot,
so that my sinking limbs may not be plunged in the muddy depths
nor my infected body be soaked in the whirlpool of vices,
but that my steps, standing firm above on the bank of virtues,
may hold fast to faith, trample on earthly joys,
and long to escape with swift effort all that flows away.
With this prayer alone let me pause a little by the river,
while, recalling them, I run through the honors of the illustrious patron,
at whose merit the flood of waters, rejoicing to submit itself
to holy commands, obeyed what it was ordered.
The fasts he kept throughout the whole year without break
were relaxed a little by the solemn feast of holy Easter.
On those days alone he afflicted his body more gently.
Only then did he take a small fish for food.
But as the occasion was being kept for signs to come,
the usual catch for this service disappointed their hopes.
When he learned that the fishermen's labor had come to nothing
and that their outstretched nets had floated through empty depths,
learning it from the complaining words and murmurs of the dejected men
(for the deacon who was present confirmed the others' account
with faithful enough words, a man whom pressing concern for this
service had kept awake through the previous night
and, weary after the part of the present day already spent,
had made a witness on the spot of their common labor),
when the deacon's anxiety stirred the saint's devout heart,
moved with devout sorrow he said: 'Go, and quickly cross
the flowing waters and search the river with skill.
Now the nets will enclose a captive prey for you.'
Without delay, trusting the word of so great a master,
the deacon hurries off. Hope is restored to his anxious wish,
and the catch, though delayed, did not fail the eager man.
For as soon as he had enclosed the nearby shallows with a small net,
the line trembled with a jolt as the cork floats bobbed,
revealing prey entangled out on the trackless blue water.
Quickly he hauled to the nearby shore, rejoicing,
the pike caught in the net. Then, bending forward with his whole body,
he wraps his wet arms around the slipping fish.
The slippery prey barely stays in his bare arms,
and, thrashing, almost slides out of his wet embrace,
until, little by little, having left its native element,
it breathed out its thin life, dying in the air,
and, quivering, opened its mouth in a feeble gape,
flapping its thrown-back tail with sluggish movement.
The monks in their joy were astonished at their wish fulfilled,
they who had come out of their neighboring cells to so great a spectacle,
favoring the outcome and believing that, with such a guarantor, the word
brought forth from the holy breast would be fulfilled.
O true mirror of eternal power! From him
these gifts flow to you, who once commanded
his disciples, weary from a night's toil in vain,
to let down their nets, sending a great prey into them,
enclosing fish chosen for the holy banquet,
those whom, snatched wholly out of the whirlpool of the world,
the teaching of the holy faith would draw to the Lord.
Often God willed that illustrious men should make known
the sublime merit of the blessed man, so that, with these
as witnesses, whom the glory of the world had raised so high,
the signs of power published among the peoples might shine more brightly.
For Arborius, then renowned for the summit of the prefecture he had held,
saw, while Martin was offering the holy rites to God,
his hand glowing, flashing with the light of shining
gems, and a gleaming light
clothing his fiery right hand in precious purple,
and he heard the crackling sound of jewels striking together.
No such stones adorned the standards of generals,
nor do such diadems encircle the brows of kings,
but such as the Lord's sentence at the end of time sets,
as well-earned gems, into the bright crowns of the saints.
Nor is there any doubt that, through the outstanding integrity of his faith,
he shone beyond what is human with a varied flowering of virtues,
he whose merit, shown in the consolation of an angel speaking face to face,
the happy page of the historical book attests.
For when he was returning in deep sorrow from the city of Trier,
where, since the emperor was angry, he feared death
for the wretched men whose lives he was begging from him,
and so, compelled to relax his own strictness a little,
he had looked more mildly upon the Ithacian offense,
driven to spare with clemency a cause he had condemned
and to renew once more the bonds of holy peace:
then, as he was overwhelmed with grief, coming to visit him,
an angel, plainly present and speaking face to face,
gently brought consolation to his grieving friend,
soothing his anxious heart with the words he offered,
teaching him by counsel what must be changed and absolving what had been done.
Even so, marking the herald of an outstanding prophet,
a heavenly messenger with holy lips made Zechariah
learn in advance of the birth of a holy son,
promising that his voice would return after the silence imposed on him.
In short, an equal sequence showed a merit not unequal:
as a son came to the one, so grace came to this man,
shining more brightly with the added light of miracles.
For often the specters were driven from a captive breast,
before ever being compelled by his words or voice in person,
terrified by the happy nearness of his holy cell
and by the power that went out far beyond his blessed dwelling.
So the signs, spreading very far, shone far and wide,
bearing witness to the Lord's present favor,
not content with land alone, but quite often bursting
far out into the very waves with Martin's honors.
Sailors tossed in an immense whirlwind saw,
while the wave of a raging storm grew ever more violent,
how much the saint could help by his name alone.
A ship was furrowing the open sea on the Tyrrhenian expanse,
speeding with sails spread across the blue water.
Its swift prow cut the depths beneath it,
breaking the white waves with the breast it set against them,
leaving long tracks of foaming paths behind,
when suddenly clouds spread across the sky and veiled it,
damp fleeces wove a blackening canopy,
and the light perished, wholly buried in pitch-black cloud.
Mighty winds set to overturning the sea,
and the drenched sands are mingled with the red waves.
Towering masses of water are shattered by the violent whirlwind.
The rolling swells, hanging high on the uplifted wave
and raising unstable hills far too high,
break apart as they fall back in crash after crash
and, collapsing, send out countless roars far and wide.
The sails fall; the rigging resounds with a quivering shriek.
Now the ship lies hidden as a mountain of water breaks off near the clouds;
now again it teeters high on a ridge, precariously poised,
fearing a perilous fall into the deep on either side;
meanwhile other waves pound the resisting sides
and, broken, rebound from the battered framework of planks,
filling the shattered ship with such constant spray.
The violence of the sea strikes off the rudder, torn away,
and flings the helmsman far off. Terror shakes
the hearts of the frightened men, convulsing their insides with trembling
and wetting their pale cheeks with more than spray.
Confused groans, the murmurs of tearful voices,
and the sighs of the weeping, broken by constant sobs,
all lament alike as death draws near.
Meanwhile a certain man, driven by extreme terror,
but not yet instructed in the teaching of the true faith,
begged for heavenly help with this cry:
'O God, unknown to me, but known through the merit of the holy
servant whom I revere, through whom your glory shines,
for Martin's sake have mercy, O God, drive away the danger,
rescue us. For the holy bishop, as I remember,
has proved by many miracles that all things are easy for you.'
At once the seas sank down, their waves laid flat,
and the plain of calm waters lay level,
and the west wind, gently driving the battered ship with a moderate breeze,
brought it to the harbor it longed for.
So Christ proved his servant's merit through all the elements
and spread abroad the honors of his holy friend,
glorifying his illustrious name over the trackless blue sea.
Nor is it a wonder that, with God's favor, Martin's faith
could be proved in so many things whenever,
wakeful in his blessed vigils, with all the strength of prayer,
he had brought his happy petitions to the Lord in person,
if, even for those wholly ignorant of him and far away,
grace was found worthy to shine through his name alone.
Although my page, striving toward his special praise,
draws back its foot in astonishment and fears with paltry
words to climb up to so great a mass of miracles,
in which the saint is shown to have healed not one man but a whole
household at once by his healing intercession,
there stands as witness Lycontius, exalted as vicar of the illustrious prefecture,
who ascribes these gifts to him with grateful lips,
whose household a single plague, raging far and wide
with manifold ruin, had overwhelmed. Everywhere the wasting
bodies of the half-dead, cast down in every part of the house,
crowded its dreadful thresholds with exhausted limbs.
Everywhere grim pain, frequent sighs, constant
weeping, and groans wrung from the very depths
of the breast, breathing that racked the inner parts,
ceaseless vomiting, parched skin, a flame lodged in the marrow
setting the stomach afire, a heavy wave of fever.
Those sorrowful bodies of the half-dead grew pale
beside a corpse close by, and the crowd of the dying,
made sadder by such an example, dreaded the funerals of their kin.
Others, poor wretches, were afraid even to touch their dead loved ones,
performing that duty with great trepidation,
lest the spreading contagion should sow grievous diseases.
Fear had withdrawn them from this service, but grief had
filled their anxious hearts with manifold mourning.
And those who had laid bodies in the most recent graves,
spared for no long time before a like death,
carried the same diseases back to the sorrowful thresholds.
Physicians' hands availed nothing, nor did herbs, which with their juices
had often worked great cures for the sick.
So the master of the house, confounded by such a disaster among his people
and distrusting his own prayers, labors to appease
the Lord through the intercession and merit of the holy patron,
pleading the woeful disaster with Martin as his advocate.
Martin, although he felt that the burden of so hard a case,
with the Judge already offended, was very great, yet anxious and merciful
he received the petitioner's prayers with solicitous affection.
Nor did he cease, tormented by unbroken toil,
to wear down his parched limbs, their marrow exhausted,
and to strike the hard ground as he lay prostrate,
doubling his usual fasts with added penances,
not closing his eyes even in light sleep,
and goading his wasted flesh with a bristly fleece,
until the Lord, moved by the zeal of so great a friend,
at last grew gentle, his wrath wholly ended,
granting the happy gifts of longed-for health,
and the crowd of his household, embracing their thankful master,
welcomed him, showing their joy with all their prayers,
as he told of the honors and deeds of the illustrious patron.
After the disaster had been driven off by Martin's prayer,
hastening thus to repay gifts to the deserving saint,
he brought a hundred pounds of silver to the aforesaid saint's threshold,
repaying his reward with the gifts he offered,
so that a fee, however small, might attest the physician's merit
and the wishes of a generous and grateful man might be shown in his zeal.
The saint, rejoicing at the kindness of his dear friend,
did not refuse these rewards that bore witness to the affection of a devoted heart,
for he carefully considered the giver's loss,
so that the gifts sent ahead might bring back the fruit of faith;
nor, on the other hand, did he take them for his own use,
lest the desire to possess should stain the saint's mind;
but, entrusting them to God, he stored them away high in heaven,
so that, by freeing captives at once from harsh punishments,
shut out from his devout threshold and given to the redeemed,
they might keep faith by being paid out and keep his strictness by being scorned.
Go on, then, following what you sent ahead, reclaiming what was promised,
O bishop, on high to the bright citadel of heaven,
you to whom a starry home and a glowing crown have been allotted,
you who were able to confine all the rage and the whole fury
of the dreadful demon in a tiny fly.
But we shall always venerate your body, present among us,
until you return with your body to eternal life,
you who are joined to the tombs of the saints and are to be joined to their crowns.
You have been able to hide from us scarcely anything but your face,
for you remain with us in loving-kindness. Crowds of people often
visit you; healing lives on in your presence;
the gifts of longed-for health are at hand at once.
Words are silent, but signs shine. If in body you are for a little while
withdrawn from sight, in power you are seen to be present.
I pray that you may be willing to be plainly present in the heart of a wretched poet
always, so that, when meditation has finished the song,
this prayer, written down, may hold fast its praise.
BOOK SIX.
You rouse my care again for songs to be begun anew,
while you prove your life by your power, O bishop not shut away
by the law of death; outliving your flesh, though without flesh,
you are seen, sought, touched and held.
While you grant present help, you show your honor,
standing by whoever seeks you, never hidden from whoever prays.
How well the spirit, close at hand, embraces the limbs nearby,
and grace floods the holy stone!
Nothing is far when faith knocks. Crying hearts
plead their own causes without voice or murmur.
He reads the words of the mind who looks into our thoughts, who visits the heart
and surveys the secret cave of the breast.
Earlier, recalling his deeds, I set them down in five books,
choosing a few out of many. What fraction
of such great glories have we learned? What can one man grasp?
With what great reward he repays a slight labor!
Again I attempt his praises with an unworthy mind:
so many prayers does my heart bear, because of my patron's goodness.
Holy grace goes before merit: the palm is held
and the burden is not felt. I have not yet tasted the toil
of the task: that he bids me be willing is already the pledge of the reward.
O how many tongues of greater eloquence
could have adorned this work with their gifts! Yet he does not allow familiar
songs to be rejected: he trusts as good the things he knows are his own.
For it is certain that he himself commanded what the interpreter he sent
thinks should be attempted—one joined to him and clinging to him
and always reverent toward the precepts of so great a master,
a blessed teacher who will live on into perpetual ages.
He does not tell the uncertainties of report, nor does he credulously
hasten to spread the breezes of rumor through listening ears.
He vouches for things seen face to face; he stands as a most faithful witness;
a champion of the faith, he makes known miracles he has examined,
presented to his own eyes and granted to prayers.
Hither from different parts of the world, vying with one another,
crowds gather; thousands multiply their countless needs
and repeat their prayers. Swift grace grants
the help of the mercy they long for. They rejoice and exult
that, their journey done, they carry away a swift fruit of their labor.
Now indeed minds possessed by a raging demon
are summoned here by help, snatched here by swift healing.
The guilty are brought to stand and they tremble. Confession cries out,
wrung out by command. Under the judge a wholesome punishment
is seen, and the invader is ordered to utter his own words
in another's body, from the captive mouth.
The judge is felt; the wicked enemy is not seen.
An exile, he hastens to leave the prey torn from him
and to vanish, fleeing amid the punishments pressing upon him.
Bonds of air bind the entangled body.
Limbs you thought were free you will marvel to see bound.
What is seen will strengthen faith. The one whom punishment has bound
shows his torments, bound more tightly with arms entwined,
and he beats against obstacles set before his fastened limbs.
What of when, as their steps rest on the chancel rails,
a path of air holds them up? Their swaying
bodies run, and the hollow air bears up the flight laid upon it.
Indeed, even into the well, which, enclosed within the church itself,
hollow, pours forth healing waters from its spring,
bodies are hurled, driven in a headlong leap,
the guilty spirit forcing them headfirst; pressing down the crown,
he thrusts the head, going before its limbs, into the depth
of the pool, and crushes the brain under the weight of the limbs.
But who would not see, when the sunken bodies rise again,
that an outstretched bosom lay open, and that the supports of favor
had opened their arms and gently caught those who fell?
The robber weighs down the limbs; mercy preserves the life.
The zeal of help is more evident than the brigand's punishment.
Whoever of you wavers with tottering faith, take heed: bodies rise again
and are drawn back to life by Martin's prayer.
The deep swallows only the limbs of the wretched,
nor does the well crush those shut within its gaping mouth.
But why do I speak of wells? A river, nursling of the place, bears witness
to a work of wonderful power—the river which, joined to the city's walls,
laps the stones with its neighboring streams.
Flowing between, it separates the cell from the tomb
and lays its broad waters between the divided places;
navigable, and spreading itself like a strait with its vast flood,
setting its banks far apart,
it wearies the eyes with the farther view
and tires even strong arms with swimming across.
To this river, from the church that holds the holy limbs
and keeps the blessed body for eternal praise,
a mad demon made his way with a wretched body,
meaning to drown the prey he had seized in the nearby flood.
But such great mercy permits nothing bloody
and takes from the dread tyrant his most savage rights.
The path is trodden as if hardened; the wave, made solid, resists
the steps and does not wash over the hurrying feet.
Across the river the crowds were astounded at the dry clothes,
and the cell joyfully received the man who was to be cleansed—
the cell that once had been the happy host of an angelic life.
Yet minds disturbed at the time retained nothing of what had been done
when they returned to themselves with their senses restored.
Often he utters the sounds of the Huns and the growls of threatening men
and words clipped short in savage abbreviations.
He received help openly before witnesses and did not know it,
unaware of the gift and saved by so great a gift.
Often the possessing spirit bent tongues to foreign sounds
and seized those of the wretched mouth,
so that Gallic words flowed out in Greek speech,
and by speaking they gave voice to a people not known even by name.
Would anyone think that this man spoke of his own understanding,
when he speaks things unknown to him? From the cave of his breast
the possessor bellows and bends the subdued tongue,
as strings sound out the movement the plectrum runs over,
and the threads of the sinews speak at the command of the hand.
O how often, under God's pressure, they confess what is to come,
and those whose lies always delight in deceit
are forced to speak the truth wrung from them by the Lord!
What a punishment it is to speak plainly! The command draws out
the voice, and the overpowered will yields to the order.
A man illustrious in valor, but in his gracious character
more renowned, and great in faith, by which he stands higher still—
Aegidius—a hostile siege had surrounded with a great host,
which had hedged in the walls with opposing arms,
shutting out help and pressing hard on those shut in,
so that division would lessen the strength of the besieged
and allied camps could not join together for war.
But by the Lord's protection the thousands are cast down and routed,
and the army, going out through the double gates,
restores its solid strength, its leader now secure.
Meanwhile the grieving countryside around, in trembling fear,
grew pale at the peril of so great a noble, and all
the anxious care of the frightened peoples hung in suspense,
while each thinks he will endure a like storm,
and all that rests on one man totters in that one.
So it happened that one of those whom a fouler fury
had drawn to long to drink blood in slaughter,
snatched up as if by a headlong whirlwind at the Lord's nod
and outstripping the swift winds across blasts and clouds,
brought forth from the captive body the course of events,
proclaiming that at those same moments, at that same time,
the city had been freed from siege through Martin's prayer,
and that God had granted him both people and leader.
Soon clear proof appeared and confirmed the account.
It was the very day, the same hour, nothing out of order,
and punishment forced the unwilling enemy not to deceive.
As Balaam, wishing to curse the Lord's people,
blessed the exulting assembly when God wrung it from him,
just so, and in exactly the same order of events, came
news that the city had been freed from a great siege—
the city that subdued the headlong Rhône with a pliant bridge
and joined its twin banks with a linked roadway,
to provide a dry path that rests on boats
from above, a swaying road hanging over the weighed-down river.
This city too, O saint, joined with the patron present there,
you rescue, and you force the trembling foe to confess your prayers,
which he would not have granted to you. The guilty one stands there, and, swifter than the east wind,
having lost his view of the slaughter he longed for,
he does not keep silent but becomes the herald of a deliverance he hates.
This too the reckoning revealed when the hours were compared:
it was accomplished and announced, as the facts showed, at the very same moment.
Now indeed, how great a healing brought remedies to all,
not by a physician's hand, not applied with a wholesome potion,
not suffering the edge of the knife or the draught of herbs,
nor seizing for the ulcer the fire of melted sulphur,
but flowing from a healing word and rightly proven
by swift power through faith, which, standing close at hand,
invites all the fearful while it heals those who reach it.
Here the blind marveled at the gift of a light unknown,
here the lame at swift running in a strengthened body,
here the deaf at the new distinctions of the voice bestowed on them:
as many causes as had brought ruin, so many gifts restore
health. Always help stands by in greater number
than the sufferings, and present protection puts danger to flight.
A paralyzed maiden experienced this great healing,
she who had afflicted her wretched parents with long grief.
For the violence of the disease had taken away
all use of her limbs; dead beforehand in all her sinews at once,
it had cast her utterly lifeless limbs upon her bed,
and, living only by her groaning, with weary breath
and faint gasps she shook her panting chest.
Carried by her parents' hands to the saint's shrine,
she lay, pitiable, near the tomb.
Now they wet their dewy faces with weeping in turn
and vie with one another in a flowing river of tears.
Mercy moved the saint. Scarcely had the light touch
of blessed oil touched the wretched limbs
when her feet leapt up, her sinews took on strength,
her strong arms felt the longed-for motion,
and her raised hands played with loosened fingers.
At once the unhappy parents seize the joys they prayed for,
and, trembling so, can scarcely believe what they would rather believe.
Her face is changed again with a happier calm,
and the new wonder of her bright countenance captivates them.
Yet integrity did not preserve this blessing for long.
Those who now burdened the threshold with constant prayers,
promising a quick return after such great rewards,
and that they would soon relieve the cost of the poor by their gifts—
the poor whom the holy bishop generously feeds and clothes,
devotedly giving his customary help to the needy,
his ready will growing rich by its own spending—
when they caught the dire poison of the ancient snake,
and the same serpent who once persuaded Eve
drove them too, by the envy of a like counsel,
to trample on neglected faith, then their perverse will,
given over to evil counsels, unhappily obeyed the words
of those who wished otherwise, turning to foul lies,
heedless and utterly forgetful of the favor they had seen.
With a mad heart it sought idolatrous rites,
changed the planned journey, and snatched the healthy girl
away from the author of life and handed her over to the dread robber,
ungrateful to faith but subject to the enemy.
But when the deceived maiden, in her error, saw from afar
the deadly shrines of the infernal tyrant,
she collapsed, and, stripped of the gift of so great a patron,
she was handed over, her body broken, to her own diseases,
until the girl who had been healed by the earlier gift
was carried off by death, doubled by her ills and owed to her punishment.
How much better if, remembering the gifts of so great a healing,
even her present life had called her to eternal life,
so that in faith she might rightly have remembered the word of the gospel,
by which the servant healed by the Lord's gift was commanded
to shun his sin, lest he go back to it again
and atone for his fault with a heavier punishment.
At times he compelled the unjust by a just terror
to feel the power of God. For often rebels,
if precepts do not yet rule them, are at least compelled by blows.
When suddenly Gaul, terrified by fear of a graver danger,
put up with the Huns as auxiliaries
(for you could scarcely bear an ally who is harsher than the enemy
and in his savagery spurns the treaty that binds him),
one of them, driven by the goads of a raging demon,
a shameless robber, burst into the Lord's holy house.
Then, daring to profane God's altar with his unholy step,
and following the frenzied desires of what he saw,
he snatched away the holy crown with a plundering right hand—
the crown which, set close by, showed forth the saint's merit,
portraying the crown he received with Christ as judge,
shining in the star-bearing citadel high in heaven.
But the eyes felt the guilt, because those lights, the heart's messengers,
had wanted to hoard the plunder they had gazed on.
Exulting, he sinned by his gaze, and could not see
what he had seized; the pleasure was withdrawn and left his eyes.
He groaned that his sight was beset as if by night in the daytime,
and, seeking the comfort of the light all around,
he grieved that the sun nearby was thickening into darkness.
Why is he amazed that his sight is shut by sudden darkness?
He was blind already when he looked wickedly on what he meant to steal.
But when he disclosed his crime to a friend who asked,
and laid bare his deeds to a companion who inquired,
following a guide who went before him as though night compelled it,
he sought the blessed altar with a different purpose,
tamed now by his own disaster and nearer to salvation.
Confessing what he had done, guilty, and wishing to condemn himself
by a wholesome judgment, he seems to have earned
pardon by this, that he confesses he earned punishment.
Grief makes amends for what deserved punishment: he restores what he seized,
so that he may regain what he lost: he takes back his own, he offers what he took.
The perverted mind received punishment; the converted mind, healing.
But another, thirsting for slaughter with more violent rage,
fiercer than the demon who, shut up within a captive body,
furiously oppressed the wretch by infernal right,
struck the body besieged by the deadly demon—
an enemy far crueler than so dread a guest—
and plunged his bloody sword into the pierced breast.
But the same persistent madness, or the same fury,
turned the foaming sword and the right hand dripping with blood
against the author of the crime, the murder scarcely done,
and with the blade laid open the hiding places of so great a crime,
searching through his bowels for the deed wickedly conceived.
How quickly swift vengeance proved the judgment,
and how speedily retribution joined itself to such a deed!
Let no one think these things harsh, since a few signs sharpen fear,
punishment terrifies, and dread is a remedy.
Rejoicing to add adornment to the holy altars,
the people hurried, vying with one another in exultant zeal.
But when this great undertaking
was attempting to move beautiful columns to the threshold of the holy church,
a certain man, rebelling with a blinded heart against such eagerness,
prepares to oppose it, or dares to delay such undertakings,
driven by the prompting of a raging demon,
and threatens his wife besides, that with her tears she would pay
for the finished work, since, living as it happened in the countryside nearby,
she had supplied tools that were wanted for the work.
Without delay, into the clear shallows of a little stream
he was thrown headlong from his horse, and he found no
waters able to drown his prostrate body.
Doomed to drown, he looked for water and lay upon the thin stream:
dying, he swallowed the sand he had pressed.
A shipwreck without a ship takes him, a flood without a river.
The elements recognize God. Nothing could afterward
be falsely put down to chance, for a command alone had done it.
Surely the tears of your wife as she wept at your funeral
were not stirred by the threats you had made; she laments because, before,
you, a prophet of a hateful omen, foretold what was to come.
You go ahead of our columns, no longer hindering them,
nor do you rob the church of its adornment—you who are to be carried off to the tomb.
But the people, devoted with greater faith and urgent,
hastened the splendid work. Power was proved,
judgment shone forth, and present devotion grew.
Now, with terror laid aside, you will read on, corrected by these perils;
you will count the kindly gifts of our outstanding patron,
and, after the poison struck down and the serpent vanquished,
you will first rejoice in the juice of nectar-sweet oil.
Whenever the nearness of the holy tomb
received it close at hand, true grace changed the liquid
and swiftly brought speedy cures.
The blessed bishop had brought and offered oil
with unhesitating faith, that the saint's spirit might moisten it
and a new breath of the neighboring favor might suffuse it:
Perpetuus, a worshiper of the Lord not in name only,
following the examples his holy master had set before him.
When, in reverence, he wished to bring this aid to people's health
and apply this proven good to every kind of cure,
dust quickly scraped from the blessed marble
and mixed with the holy oil doubled its powers,
so that the power, thus redoubled in the sprinkled liquid,
might increase faith by its touch and health by its union.
But when the oil felt the nearness of even a tiny grain,
swift grace lifted the oil it touched,
and a swelling overflow boiled up. The abundance grew,
for the gift increased before their eyes as it was brought out.
Rising above its rim, the outpouring wet the stopper.
And yet the overflowing grace caused no loss,
flowing over what lay beneath and ever full though vessels were filled.
This glory never stains the garments it soaks:
once seen, they keep a brightness greater than Siloam's,
bearing witness to so great a work. Let no one wash out
what power has marked and inscribed with such a sign.
Nor is this praise confined to one place: grace followed the faithful
and sent the saint's lofty glories even into the air.
The very storms felt the saint's merit;
the terror of hail stayed fixed in the thickened clouds,
and a gentler wrath spared places marked for ruin.
A certain man, confident he would bring home true safety
if he were allowed to carry something from the threshold of the saint's church
to his own house, a faithful servant, joyfully received
the healing reward of blessed wax.
His glad faith experienced what it had felt with all his heart:
the hope he cherished brought back help.
His field, protected, escaped those darts of water,
hard as stone, the icy lashes of frozen rain,
for it shielded the crops by this sowing, which, buried in the earth,
spread wide branches to give the shelter prayed for.
The whole neighborhood was astonished at the favor granted,
and the power already known was revealed by true signs.
Not with a hundred tongues could I tell all these praises
or unfold such great triumphs of miraculous power.
I need not knock at the oracles of lying Phoebus,
nor wait for the lyres of the invented sisters.
Let another fill us for the proclaiming of so great a praise:
let the Spirit give words and joy to our heart.
That I may sing the truth, let my patron be my Muse;
let him cherish me and let his grace quicken my mind,
lest I be overcome by the splendor of the work, or, overwhelmed
by so great a light, turn my unsteady eyes away from it;
and let me sing high and heavenly things with clear understanding.
Reader, believe the holy God in what you hesitate
to believe from us, and you will know that all these things are easy for Christ,
who gave them and commanded them to add to the saint's glories.
Every year the people were accustomed to pay solemn homage to the holy man,
when the circle of the returning year
joyfully renewed the mysteries of holy Easter.
Deep veneration for the cell draws them in haste—
the cell that lay open as a faithful host to so eminent a saint,
possessed by an angelic man. Bowed faces grow wet
with weeping, and with tears they seek the saint's footsteps.
What places he touched as he sang psalms, what spots he pressed as he prayed,
they wish to recall here; where he took his food,
breaking his immense fasts with a scanty taste;
which cell, with heavenly help, gave him rest from his vigils
and, granting brief sleep to his limbs,
refreshed his lofty mind with waking visions.
Hither the shepherd joyfully delights to lead his people.
He ferries the crowd across, taken aboard many boats,
and the waves are hidden beneath the fleet. Here every sex and age
is present. Houses stand empty of guardians;
mutual trust stands watch over all their homes.
Meanwhile the author of death and sin, filled
with the spite of his envy, prepares to oppose these efforts,
and, attacking a heavily laden boat,
sank it in mid-stream in the vast flood,
wrapping all he had seized together in the deep
and dragging the entangled crowd along in the river's current.
What a disaster he expected, exulting! With what triumph
he counted the longed-for deaths of a countless multitude,
tearing little ones from their nurses' breasts
and scattering the drifting wreckage over the trackless blue,
seeing others, their necks weighed down by an embrace,
sink under the body their arms had clasped,
and others, their clothes already soaked, dragged down, yet seeking heaven
with their eyes and with their murmurs driving back the water that poured in.
Meanwhile a united cry in Martin's name
calls on heavenly help. The whole crowd
falls prostrate and floods the damp sand with weeping.
So joyful a day owed special joys to the grieving
and an outstanding gift at that solemn season.
At once a gentler spirit was present in the midst of the waves
and snatched away the wicked rights of cruel death.
The water held up the drifting limbs. Made firm for their safety,
the flood bore the bodies up on its waters. Not struck by swimming,
not furrowed and wounded by alternating strokes of hands,
it carried its motionless burden and brought back to the banks
their joys, and gladly counted the safety it had borne.
The mother recognized her son, the infant clung to its mother,
and the father clasped his children in his embrace.
Brother, mother, master, servant, matron, kinsman
came running together, and a resounding voice
sang thanks and praised God in holy hymns.
Scarcely does anyone dare at once to believe what they saw;
with trembling prayer each questions his doubting eyes.
Yet faith was not broken by terror: they hasten to the river.
New grace swiftly restores their vigorous strength.
They have no wish to change their dress. In the same clothes
they exult, and faith is not chilled by a wet cloak.
So the farther bank, rejoicing in so great a triumph,
said gladly and in faith, "Let us sing to the Lord."
The prey sings unharmed; the plunderer stayed drowned.
Behold, once more the Lord split open the Jordan's waters,
opened a divided path, and bade the people go through the river
close behind the ark that went before them.
Returning to its source, the flood turned back its streams,
and, halting its course, hurried backward toward its rising.
The people wore down these places, treading the sands
over which the anxious sailor had sped with oar and sail.
What paths of land and sea has the glory of this name
not reached, sped on by a swift leap,
passing over the sea-lanes and the backs of the vast ocean
open to sailors? A ship, swept away by violent storms
and carried far into an unknown deep,
beyond the routes of men and fleets, had burst headlong,
driven by a whirlwind, into a sea bound fast in torpor.
No hope offered escape. For with its gluey water
the sea, motionless and resisting, held the planks
in a siege of the sea. Longing for winds, the sailors
would have welcomed the help of a tempest and the wrath of a whirlwind,
praying for a storm in the midst of the waves.
But the wretched men are given no means of escape.
So sluggish a shipwreck holds them, without any motion.
The ship that floats on the sea cannot float away. A hateful stillness
clings in the waves. What the sea holds up, it hinders;
it neither drives the ship onward nor swallows it in a chasm.
No hope of escape appears. For in the waves
a sluggish guard keeps the prey bound fast by the water.
The one hope is God alone. Whatever he created,
he also rules. The elements obey their Creator's command.
At the Lord's nod things suddenly stirred grow still,
things sluggish swiftly learn unaccustomed motion,
and his command gives law to things he ordered long before.
One man, following report with better judgment,
had learned of Martin's glories as fame spread them through the world,
and of his miracles, full of holy deeds.
Driven by misfortune, thinking the only safety
lay in crying out to the true God, he prayed thus:
he lifted to heaven eyes wet with a fountain of tears
and, joining the depths of his heart to his eyes,
said, "Look upon the wretched, O one true hope of salvation.
Have mercy, God of Martin, you who through him
have scattered so many signs of divine favor among the peoples,
and, proving his merit by power, have bidden his glories
pass beyond the lands and be famous even across the seas.
By his prayers let him loose or slacken the bonds of the ship,
force the waters to part and give way,
and at last make the sea thin and flowing in its depths."
Without delay a mighty wind swept swiftly down
and drove out the captive ship, cleaving the flood,
and carried it with an easy breeze over the trackless blue,
and soon gave rest in the longed-for haven of a port
to those carried out and carried home again in Martin's name,
as with steadfast faith they sang of the gifts their prayers had won.
Who, then, can grasp these things in thought? Who can paint them in song?
Who could count them, who could set them forth? Everything is surpassed
every talent; the task of proclaiming them silences tongues weighed down.
Even so, though I fall short of the titles that glory attends,
the things I have learned, or so often reread in writing,
since I cannot speak of them as is fitting, I will at least try to touch on.
A certain man, returning to his own doorstep from the saint's holy church,
believing that he was bringing his house a safeguard of salvation,
had carried home with him into its inner rooms some holy wax,
trusting that the blessing of so great a patron, joined to it,
would be present in power because of the merits of such righteous faith.
And now the time had come for proofs of that favour to be shown.
It happened that, through a fire that had escaped, a ravenous flame crept carelessly along
and, swelling its strength on the fuel of the timber,
was already pressing the house toward ruin. On every side a dense smoke
was rolling a surging mass up into the air in a whirlwind.
It swallowed whatever was dry, seizing it and licking at all in its path,
and leaving nothing but ashes from so great a disaster.
Nor was there hope of escape as the danger blazed ever nearer.
Terror, looming close to the inner rooms, had hemmed them in,
and the dangers nearby had closed around a prey so near at hand.
Their prayers turned back to the saint. With a faithful cry
he is called upon, and voice after voice repeats his holy name.
The master himself seizes the glowing lights of the kindled wax,
which shed a gentle light from their blessed richness,
and with a swift and trembling right hand rushes them to the inner rooms;
and setting the burning tapers in the very midst of the flames,
with the protection of fire he drove back the onrushing fire.
The raging whirlwind halted. At once the destroying enemy
turned its back, and a spark put to flight the fury of the fire.
Not even if the clouds had flung down all their rainstorms
could tempests poured from above have done such good,
nor, if crowds vying with one another had carried off whole rivers,
could any springs, though the river were drained dry,
have brought help so swiftly as did true power.
The fire, trembling, flees the wax that is its own fuel,
and nature, in harmony, dreads the honeycombs that nourish it.
By its power the wax destroys the flame it feeds with its light,
fragrant with the clear nectar of its rich liquid.
I have dared to run quickly through these things in a few words,
and, unlearned as I am, I have set them down for the faithful people to read again.
Joys so great have strengthened my humble voice.
What you complain is poorly described, you will marvel at as deeds done.
It is enough that, scorning the acclaim of my poem, you should praise this:
that death has had no power, since life is openly proved.
The city of Tours rejoices for ever in Martin its bishop.
